Item Response Theory with mirt and mirtverse Notes for teaching and learning Okan Bulut Measurement, Evaluation, and Data Science University of Alberta E-mail: bulut@ualberta.ca Website: www.okanbulut.com November 2026 Preface This book is a set of extended course notes on item response theory (IRT). It is written for instructors who teach measurement with R and for the students in their courses. Every chapter mixes a short explanation of the ideas with worked examples that you can run line by line, using the mirt package (Chalmers 2012) for estimation and mirtverse for model choice, tidy tables, graphics and plain-language interpretation. How the book is organised The twelve chapters follow the twelve weeks of the mirtverse course map, so an instructor can assign one chapter a week and pair it with the matching lab. Chapter 1 Measurement, scoring and classical item analysis Learning goals. After this chapter you can turn raw responses into item scores with a key, and reverse-score negatively worded items; compute and read proportion correct, item-total correlations and coefficient alpha; use a distractor analysis to spot an item that is miskeyed or badly written; say what a sum score can and cannot tell you, and why we need IRT. Key terms: classical test theory, sum score, p-value, item-total correlation, dichotomous item, polytomous item. 1.1 The ideas A test is a sample of tasks that we use to make an inference about something we cannot see directly: a student’s reading ability, a nurse’s clinical knowledge, a patient’s level of anxiety. Before any model is fitted, raw responses have to be turned into item scores. For a multiple-choice item that means comparing the option chosen with the key (1 = right, 0 = wrong). For a rating scale it means coding the categories as 0, 1, 2, … and making sure that a higher score always means “more” of the trait, which is why negatively worded items are reverse-scored. The simplest summary of a person’s performance is the sum score, the total of the item scores. Classical test theory (CTT) models the sum score as a true score plus error, \(X = T + E\), and gives us a small toolkit for judging items (Crocker and Algina 1986): Item difficulty (\(p\)): the proportion of people who answer correctly (for rating items, the item mean). Confusingly, a high \(p\) means an easy item. Item discrimination: the correlation between the item score and the total score. Items that good performers get right and weak performers get wrong have high item-total correlations. The corrected correlation removes the item from the total first, which matters for short tests. Coefficient alpha: an estimate of reliability, the proportion of sum-score variance that is true-score variance. Distractor analysis: for multiple-choice items, how often each wrong option is chosen, and by whom. A good distractor attracts low scorers. An option that attracts high scorers is a warning sign: it may be a second correct answer, or the key may be wrong. CTT statistics are easy to compute and to explain, and you should always start with them. But they have two limits that motivate the rest of this book. First, \(p\) and the item-total correlation depend on the group that took the test: the same item looks easy in a strong group and hard in a weak one. Second, the sum score treats every item as equally informative and gives one standard error for everybody, even though a test measures some people more precisely than others. Item response theory addresses both. 1.2 Example 1: a multiple-choice science test The SAT12 data in mirt hold the answers of 600 high-school students to 32 multiple-choice science items with five options (8 marks an omitted item). The key is published on the help page, ?SAT12. # Raw multiple-choice responses (options 1-5, 8 = omitted) and the key. raw <- SAT12 key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,5) key2binary() scores every response against the key. Omits count as wrong. resp <- key2binary(raw, key) resp[1:5, 1:8] #> Item.1 Item.2 Item.3 Item.4 Item.5 Item.6 Item.7 Item.8 #> [1,] 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 #> [2,] 0 1 0 0 1 0 1 0 #> [3,] 1 1 1 0 1 0 1 0 #> [4,] 0 1 0 1 1 0 1 0 #> [5,] 0 1 1 1 1 0 1 1 total <- rowSums(resp) summary(total) #> Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. #> 4.0 14.8 18.0 18.2 22.0 32.0 itemstats() gives the classical statistics for every item in one table. st <- itemstats(resp) st$overall #> N mean.total sd.total std.alpha alpha SEM.alpha mean.r sd.r #> 600 18.2 5.05 0.795 0.798 2.27 0.108 0.075 head(st$itemstats, 8) #> N K mean sd cor_if_rm smc alpha_if_rm #> Item.1 600 2 0.283 0.451 0.300 0.158 0.793 #> Item.2 600 2 0.568 0.496 0.464 0.270 0.785 #> Item.3 600 2 0.280 0.449 0.371 0.184 0.789 #> Item.4 600 2 0.378 0.485 0.235 0.145 0.796 #> Item.5 600 2 0.620 0.486 0.340 0.197 0.791 #> Item.6 600 2 0.160 0.367 0.351 0.185 0.791 #> Item.7 600 2 0.760 0.427 0.289 0.200 0.793 #> Item.8 600 2 0.202 0.402 0.233 0.116 0.795 The mean column is the proportion correct, cor_if_rm is the corrected item-total correlation, and alpha_if_rm is alpha with the item removed. Let us sort the items by their corrected correlation and look at the weakest. items <- st$itemstats items[order(items$cor_if_rm), c("mean", "cor_if_rm", "alpha_if_rm")][1:5, ] #> mean cor_if_rm alpha_if_rm #> Item.32 0.162 0.037 0.802 #> Item.12 0.415 0.076 0.803 #> Item.9 0.885 0.127 0.798 #> Item.21 0.915 0.136 0.798 #> Item.11 0.983 0.156 0.797 A corrected correlation near zero, or an alpha that goes up when the item is removed, means the item is not measuring what the rest of the test measures. Before blaming the item writer, check the key. A distractor analysis splits students into groups by total score and shows which option each group chose. distractors <- function(raw, total, item, groups = 5) { band <- cut(rank(total, ties.method = "first"), groups, labels = c("lowest", paste0("band ", 2:(groups - 1)), "highest")) round(prop.table(table(band, option = raw[[item]]), 1), 2) } distractors(raw, total, "Item.32") #> option #> band 1 2 3 4 5 8 #> lowest 0.12 0.26 0.35 0.09 0.14 0.04 #> band 2 0.10 0.31 0.36 0.07 0.14 0.02 #> band 3 0.19 0.16 0.42 0.08 0.15 0.00 #> band 4 0.16 0.12 0.48 0.08 0.16 0.00 #> highest 0.06 0.07 0.62 0.04 0.22 0.00 The keyed answer to item 32 is option 5, yet option 3 is the most popular choice in every band, and its share climbs steeply from the lowest band to the highest. Option 5 gains far less. When an “unkeyed” option behaves the way a correct answer should, suspect the key. The help page for SAT12 agrees: the key for item 32 is probably wrong and should be 3. Re-scoring fixes the item: key_fixed <- replace(key, 32, 3) resp_fixed <- key2binary(raw, key_fixed) st_fixed <- itemstats(resp_fixed) c(old_r = items["Item.32", "cor_if_rm"], new_r = st_fixed$itemstats["Item.32", "cor_if_rm"], old_alpha = st$overall$alpha, new_alpha = st_fixed$overall$alpha) #> old_r new_r old_alpha new_alpha #> 0.0371 0.2026 0.7979 0.8023 What to take away. A low item-total correlation is a symptom, not a diagnosis. The distractor table tells you why: a wrong key, two defensible answers, an option that confuses strong students, or simply an item that is too hard for everyone. 1.3 Example 2: a wellbeing questionnaire Rating scales need the same care. Here we simulate a short questionnaire: 800 adults rate eight statements about their wellbeing from 0 (strongly disagree) to 3 (strongly agree). Items 3 and 7 are negatively worded (“I often feel tense”), so agreeing with them means lower wellbeing. # Simulated 8-item wellbeing scale, 0-3, items W3 and W7 negatively worded. set.seed(101) a <- matrix(c(1.6, 1.4, 1.2, 1.8, 1.3, 1.5, 1.1, 0.5)) d <- matrix(c( 2.0, 0.5, -1.5, 1.8, 0.2, -1.8, 2.2, 0.8, -1.0, 1.5, 0.0, -2.0, 2.5, 1.0, -0.8, 1.7, 0.3, -1.6, 2.0, 0.6, -1.2, 1.0, 0.0, -1.0), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE) resp <- simdata(a, d, N = 800, itemtype = "graded") colnames(resp) <- paste0("W", 1:8) resp[, c("W3", "W7")] <- 3 - resp[, c("W3", "W7")] # as answered on the form resp <- as.data.frame(resp) If we forget to reverse-score, the two negative items correlate negatively with the total, and alpha is badly understated. itemstats(resp)$itemstats[, c("mean", "cor_if_rm")] #> mean cor_if_rm #> W1 1.64 0.348 #> W2 1.49 0.341 #> W3 1.24 -0.412 #> W4 1.44 0.326 #> W5 1.88 0.296 #> W6 1.60 0.356 #> W7 1.29 -0.433 #> W8 1.48 0.122 itemstats(resp)$overall$alpha #> [1] 0.224 Reverse-scoring maps 0 to 3, 1 to 2 and so on: scored <- resp scored[, c("W3", "W7")] <- 3 - scored[, c("W3", "W7")] st <- itemstats(scored) st$itemstats[, c("mean", "cor_if_rm", "alpha_if_rm")] #> mean cor_if_rm alpha_if_rm #> W1 1.64 0.543 0.710 #> W2 1.49 0.459 0.725 #> W3 1.76 0.451 0.727 #> W4 1.44 0.538 0.710 #> W5 1.88 0.443 0.728 #> W6 1.60 0.507 0.716 #> W7 1.71 0.473 0.723 #> W8 1.48 0.210 0.773 st$overall$alpha #> [1] 0.753 All items now point the same way. Item W8 still has a low corrected correlation, and alpha rises from 0.75 to 0.77 without it: it is a weak item, and an IRT model will give it a low discrimination too (Chapter 2). For rating scales the category frequencies are worth a look as well. A category almost nobody uses carries little information and may need to be merged with its neighbour (Chapter 8). round(st$proportions, 2) #> 0 1 2 3 #> W1 0.19 0.23 0.34 0.24 #> W2 0.24 0.24 0.32 0.20 #> W3 0.16 0.22 0.33 0.30 #> W4 0.26 0.26 0.27 0.21 #> W5 0.12 0.21 0.35 0.32 #> W6 0.20 0.23 0.33 0.23 #> W7 0.17 0.22 0.34 0.27 #> W8 0.27 0.25 0.20 0.28 1.4 A first look with mirtverse profile_data() gives a quick overview of any response file, and is what mv_ask() uses before it writes an analysis. For each column it reports the type, the number of distinct values, the range and the share of missing values, and it guesses which columns are items and which are IDs or grouping variables. profile_data(scored) #> Data profile: 800 rows, 8 columns (8 look like items) #> column type n_distinct min max prop_missing role levels #> W1 integer 4 0 3 0 item #> W2 integer 4 0 3 0 item #> W3 integer 4 0 3 0 item #> W4 integer 4 0 3 0 item #> W5 integer 4 0 3 0 item #> W6 integer 4 0 3 0 item #> W7 integer 4 0 3 0 item #> W8 integer 4 0 3 0 item 1.5 Your turn Score SAT12 with the corrected key. Which three items are now the hardest, and which three have the lowest corrected item-total correlation? Run distractors() on the item with the lowest corrected correlation. Is the problem the key, a distractor, or the difficulty of the item? In Example 2, what happens to alpha if you drop W8? Would you drop it? Give one reason for and one against. Suppose 30% of students omitted the last five items of SAT12 because they ran out of time. Why would scoring omits as wrong distort the item statistics of those items? Solutions resp_fixed <- key2binary(SAT12, replace(key, 32, 3)) it <- itemstats(resp_fixed)$itemstats rownames(it)[order(it$mean)][1:3] # hardest #> [1] "Item.6" "Item.8" "Item.3" rownames(it)[order(it$cor_if_rm)][1:3] # weakest #> [1] "Item.12" "Item.9" "Item.21" Use distractors(SAT12, rowSums(resp_fixed), "<item>"). If no option is preferred by the top band and the correct option rises only slowly, the item is simply hard or vague rather than miskeyed. Alpha rises only a little. Dropping W8 shortens the scale and may remove content the scale is meant to cover; keeping it costs little precision. A content review should decide, not alpha alone. Not-reached items would look harder and would correlate with speed rather than knowledge. Treat not-reached items as missing (NA) rather than wrong; IRT estimation handles missing responses naturally. You score the responses, screen the items and decide what to do about anything suspicious. See Teaching labs. Further reading Crocker and Algina (1986) remain the classic introduction to classical test theory and item analysis. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (American Educational Research Association et al. 2014) set out what evidence a test score needs before it is used. References

Chapter 2 The Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models Learning goals. After this chapter you can explain what a latent trait is and why IRT puts people and items on the same scale; write down the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models and say what each parameter does to the item characteristic curve; fit the three models with mirt() and read their parameters in the traditional IRT metric; describe an item in words from its curve. Key terms: item response theory, latent trait, logit, Rasch model, 2PL, 3PL, item characteristic curve, difficulty, discrimination, guessing, slope-intercept form. 2.1 The ideas IRT assumes that a person’s responses depend on an unobserved latent trait \(\theta\) (theta): ability, knowledge, an attitude. By convention \(\theta\) has mean 0 and standard deviation 1 in the calibration group, so a person at \(\theta = 1\) is one standard deviation above average. Each item gets an item characteristic curve (ICC): the probability of a correct answer as a function of \(\theta\). The three classic models differ in how many parameters shape that curve (Hambleton et al. 1991; Embretson and Reise 2000). The Rasch (1PL) model has one parameter per item, the difficulty \(b_j\): \[P(X_{ij} = 1 \mid \theta_i) = \frac{\exp(\theta_i - b_j)}{1 + \exp(\theta_i - b_j)}.\] The difficulty is the point on the \(\theta\) scale where the probability is 0.5. All curves have the same slope, so they never cross, and the sum score contains all the information about \(\theta\). The two-parameter logistic (2PL) model adds a discrimination \(a_j\): \[P(X_{ij} = 1 \mid \theta_i) = \frac{\exp[a_j(\theta_i - b_j)]}{1 + \exp[a_j(\theta_i - b_j)]}.\] A larger \(a_j\) gives a steeper curve: the item separates people just below \(b_j\) from people just above it more sharply. Values between about 0.8 and 2.5 are typical for good achievement items; values below about 0.5 mean the item hardly tells people apart. The three-parameter logistic (3PL) model adds a lower asymptote \(c_j\), often called the guessing parameter: \[P(X_{ij} = 1 \mid \theta_i) = c_j + (1 - c_j)\frac{\exp[a_j(\theta_i - b_j)]}{1 + \exp[a_j(\theta_i - b_j)]}.\] Even very low-ability people get a multiple-choice item right with probability \(c_j\), roughly one over the number of options if they guess at random. With a lower asymptote, \(b_j\) is where the probability is \((1 + c_j)/2\) rather than 0.5. mirt estimates the models in slope-intercept form, \(a_j\theta_i + d_j\), which behaves better numerically. The two forms are related by \(b_j = -d_j / a_j\). Use coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE), or mirtverse’s tidy() (which uses IRTpars = TRUE by default), to see \(a\) and \(b\). 2.2 Example 1: the LSAT section 7 items LSAT7 holds the response patterns of 1,000 people to five items from a section of the Law School Admission Test, stored as a frequency table. expand.table() turns it into one row per person. # Five dichotomous LSAT items, one row per test taker. resp <- expand.table(LSAT7) We fit the three models. itemtype chooses the model and verbose = FALSE hides the iteration history. rasch <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE) twopl <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) threepl <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE) The item parameters in the IRT metric: coef(twopl, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items #> a b g u #> Item.1 0.988 -1.879 0 1 #> Item.2 1.081 -0.748 0 1 #> Item.3 1.706 -1.058 0 1 #> Item.4 0.765 -0.635 0 1 #> Item.5 0.736 -2.520 0 1 The columns g and u are the lower and upper asymptotes, fixed at 0 and 1 for the 2PL. The same information as a tidy table, ready for a report: tidy(twopl) #> # A tibble: 10 × 5 #> item itemtype term estimate std.error #> <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 Item.1 2PL a 0.988 NA #> 2 Item.1 2PL b -1.88 NA #> 3 Item.2 2PL a 1.08 NA #> 4 Item.2 2PL b -0.748 NA #> 5 Item.3 2PL a 1.71 NA #> 6 Item.3 2PL b -1.06 NA #> 7 Item.4 2PL a 0.765 NA #> 8 Item.4 2PL b -0.635 NA #> 9 Item.5 2PL a 0.736 NA #> 10 Item.5 2PL b -2.52 NA All five items have negative difficulties: this is an easy section for this group. Item 3 has the steepest slope, items 4 and 5 the flattest. The curves show it at a glance. gg_trace(twopl, facet = FALSE) Figure 2.1: Item characteristic curves of the 2PL model for the five LSAT7 items. Compare the Rasch curves, which are parallel by construction, with the 2PL curves, which are not: library(patchwork) (gg_trace(rasch, facet = FALSE) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Rasch")) + (gg_trace(twopl, facet = FALSE) + ggplot2::ggtitle("2PL")) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") Figure 2.2: Rasch curves (left) are parallel by construction; 2PL curves (right) can differ in slope. The 3PL adds a lower asymptote for each item. With only five easy items there is very little information about what low-ability people do. Look at the \(c\) estimates (g) and their confidence intervals: threepl_se <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "3PL", SE = TRUE, verbose = FALSE) tidy(threepl_se, conf.int = TRUE) |> subset(term == "g") #> # A tibble: 5 × 7 #> item itemtype term estimate std.error conf.low conf.high #> <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 Item.1 3PL g 0.0000703 0.00930 -0.0182 0.0183 #> 2 Item.2 3PL g 0.295 0.140 0.0209 0.569 #> 3 Item.3 3PL g 0.000258 0.0278 -0.0543 0.0548 #> 4 Item.4 3PL g 0.0000506 0.00435 -0.00847 0.00857 #> 5 Item.5 3PL g 0.000155 0.0209 -0.0408 0.0411 Four of the five lower asymptotes sit at essentially zero, on the boundary of the parameter space, and the one that does not (Item 2) has a confidence interval that runs from almost 0 to well over 0.5. The data say very little about guessing. Which model should we report? That is a question for Chapter 3. For now, notice that a model with more parameters is not automatically better: it has to be supported by the data. interpret() describes the fitted model in plain language. Its Items section is a useful check on your own reading of the curves. interpret(twopl) #> Overview #> -------- #> * A 2PL model with 1 dimension was fitted to 1000 respondents and 5 items (EM #> estimation). #> * The estimation converged normally. #> #> Model fit #> --------- #> * Overall model fit is close: M2 = 11.94, df = 5, RMSEA = 0.037, CFI = 0.968, #> SRMSR = 0.032. #> * The chi-square test is significant, but with large samples this is common; #> the RMSEA indicates the misfit is small in practical terms. #> #> Reliability #> ----------- #> * Marginal reliability is 0.44 (low). #> * Scores are too imprecise for decisions about individuals; consider adding #> items or using the scores only for group-level summaries. #> #> Targeting #> --------- #> * The average item location is -1.37 and the average person score is 0.00, so #> the test is relatively easy for this group. #> * Measurement is most precise around theta = -1.08 (information = 1.47, SE = #> 0.83). #> #> Items #> ----- #> * Low item-total correlation: Item.5 (r = 0.17). These items relate weakly to #> the rest of the test. #> * Misfit: Item.2 (S-X2 p < .001). The model does not describe responses to #> these items well (alpha = 0.01); inspect them with gg_empirical() or #> item_card(). #> #> Local dependence #> ---------------- #> * No item pairs show signs of local dependence (Q3). #> #> Person fit #> ---------- #> * 2.1% of respondents have unusual response patterns (Zh < -1.96), which is #> within what chance alone would produce. 2.3 Example 2: a driving theory test with guessing To see when the 3PL matters, we simulate a 20-item driving theory test with four options per question, taken by 3,000 learner drivers. Because we simulate, we know the true parameters and can check how well each model recovers them. # Simulated 20-item, four-option test with real guessing (c around 0.2). set.seed(202) n_items <- 20 true <- data.frame(a = rlnorm(n_items, 0.2, 0.25), b = seq(-1.5, 2, length.out = n_items), c = rbeta(n_items, 5, 17)) resp <- simdata(a = matrix(true$a), d = matrix(-true$a * true$b), N = 3000, itemtype = "3PL", guess = true$c) colnames(resp) <- sprintf("D%02d", 1:n_items) The data chunk converts the true \(b\) into an intercept with \(d = -ab\), because simdata() uses the slope-intercept form. fit2 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) fit3 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE) est2 <- coef(fit2, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items est3 <- coef(fit3, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items recovery <- data.frame( model = rep(c("2PL", "3PL"), each = 2), parameter = rep(c("a", "b"), 2), bias = c(mean(est2[, "a"] - true$a), mean(est2[, "b"] - true$b), mean(est3[, "a"] - true$a), mean(est3[, "b"] - true$b)), rmse = c(sqrt(mean((est2[, "a"] - true$a)^2)), sqrt(mean((est2[, "b"] - true$b)^2)), sqrt(mean((est3[, "a"] - true$a)^2)), sqrt(mean((est3[, "b"] - true$b)^2)))) recovery #> model parameter bias rmse #> 1 2PL a -0.4681 0.583 #> 2 2PL b -0.5731 0.698 #> 3 3PL a 0.0622 0.338 #> 4 3PL b -0.0188 0.379 When people really do guess, the 2PL absorbs the guessing into the other parameters: it underestimates discrimination and makes hard items look easier than they are. The 3PL recovers the parameters much better, and its lower asymptotes are close to the truth on average: c(mean_true_c = mean(true$c), mean_estimated_c = mean(est3[, "g"])) #> mean_true_c mean_estimated_c #> 0.239 0.226 The empirical item curve makes the problem visible. For the hardest item, the observed proportions correct for low-ability groups sit well above the 2PL curve, which heads towards zero: gg_empirical(fit2, "D20") + gg_empirical(fit3, "D20") Figure 2.3: Empirical item curve of the hardest driving-test item, D20, under the 2PL (left) and the 3PL (right). What to take away. The 3PL is worth its extra parameters when items can be answered by guessing and there are enough low-ability test takers to estimate the lower asymptote: here 3,000 people and a range of difficulties. With small samples or easy tests, \(c\) is poorly determined, and a 2PL (or a 3PL with a prior on \(c\)) is often the safer choice. 2.4 Your turn Using the 2PL for LSAT7, compute by hand the probability that a person at \(\theta = -1\) answers Item 3 correctly. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. #> -0.3425 -0.0895 0.0558 0.0270 0.1615 0.3461 Items whose 2PL slope is far from the common Rasch slope move most, here Item 3 (the steepest) and Item 5 (one of the flattest). A flat item (small \(a\)) has a 2PL difficulty further from zero, because its curve only reaches 0.5 far out on the scale. Chapter 3 Estimation and comparing models Learning goals. After this chapter you can describe marginal maximum likelihood estimation in words; check whether a model has converged, and know what to do when it has not; compare nested models with a likelihood-ratio test and any models with information criteria; judge overall model fit with M2, RMSEA, SRMSR and CFI; explain why AIC and BIC can disagree, and what sample size has to do with it. Key terms: calibration, marginal maximum likelihood, convergence, standard error, likelihood-ratio test, information criteria, M2, RMSEA, SRMSR, CFI and TLI. 3.1 The ideas Calibration means estimating the item parameters. We never observe \(\theta\), so we cannot simply regress responses on it. Marginal maximum likelihood (MML) instead assumes a distribution for \(\theta\) in the population, usually standard normal, and integrates it out: the likelihood of a response pattern is its probability averaged over all possible values of \(\theta\). The item parameters are chosen to make the observed patterns as likely as possible (Bock and Aitkin 1981). mirt maximizes this likelihood with the EM algorithm by default. It replaces the integral with a sum over a grid of quadrature points and alternates two steps: the E-step works out, for every person, how likely each grid point is given their responses and the current item parameters; the M-step updates each item’s parameters as if those expected counts were data. The cycles stop when the parameters stop changing, which is called convergence. If the algorithm hits its limit of 500 cycles first, mirt warns you, and the estimates should not be trusted. Once a model has converged, we compare it with alternatives. Likelihood-ratio test (LRT). For nested models (the Rasch model is a 2PL with equal slopes; the 2PL is a 3PL with \(c = 0\)), twice the difference in log-likelihoods is approximately chi-square distributed with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in the number of parameters. With large samples even trivial improvements become significant. Information criteria. \(\text{AIC} = -2\log L + 2k\) and \(\text{BIC} = -2\log L + k\log N\), where \(k\) is the number of parameters and \(N\) the sample size. Smaller is better. BIC punishes extra parameters more heavily once \(N > 7\), so it favours simpler models. A difference of 10 or more BIC points is usually read as strong evidence. Absolute fit. The M2 statistic (Maydeu-Olivares and Joe 2006) compares observed and expected proportions for single items and pairs of items. RMSEA (below about 0.05 is close fit), SRMSR (below about 0.05) and CFI (above about 0.95) are effect sizes built from it. Treat the cut-offs as rough guides, not rules. 3.2 Example 1: a test the Rasch model fits LSAT6 is another five-item section of the Law School Admission Test, with 1,000 test takers. It is a textbook example of data the Rasch model fits well. # Five dichotomous LSAT items, one row per test taker. resp <- expand.table(LSAT6) Fit the models one at a time, check convergence, and compare them: rasch <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE) twopl <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) extract.mirt(rasch, "converged") #> [1] TRUE extract.mirt(twopl, "iterations") #> [1] 22 anova(rasch, twopl) #> AIC SABIC HQ BIC logLik X2 df p #> rasch 4946 4956 4957 4975 -2467 #> twopl 4953 4971 4972 5002 -2467 0.569 4 0.966 The 2PL improves the log-likelihood by a fraction of a point for four extra parameters, so the LRT is far from significant and both AIC and BIC prefer the Rasch model. glance() adds the absolute fit statistics: glance(rasch)[, c("logLik", "AIC", "BIC", "M2", "df", "p.value", "RMSEA", "SRMSR", "CFI")] #> # A tibble: 1 × 9 #> logLik AIC BIC M2 df p.value RMSEA SRMSR CFI #> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 -2467. 4946. 4975. 5.29 9 0.808 0 0.0224 1 select_model() runs all of this in one call. It fits the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models (or the polytomous equivalents), checks convergence, ranks them by BIC, runs the LRTs between nested pairs and explains its recommendation. sel <- select_model(resp, verbose = FALSE) sel #> mirtverse model selection (ranked by BIC) #> #> model npar logLik AIC BIC SABIC RMSEA CFI delta weight #> Rasch 6 -2467 4946 4975 4956 0 1 0.0 1 #> 2PL 10 -2467 4953 5002 4971 0 1 27.1 0 #> 3PL 15 -2467 4963 5037 4989 NA NA 61.6 0 #> #> The Rasch model is recommended because it has the lowest BIC (4975.3). The #> runner-up, 2PL, is 27.1 BIC points worse, which is very strong evidence for the #> Rasch model. Likelihood-ratio test Rasch vs. 2PL: chi-square(4) = 0.57, p = #> .966; the extra parameters of 2PL are not needed. Likelihood-ratio test Rasch #> vs. 3PL: chi-square(9) = 0.54, p = 1.000; the extra parameters of 3PL are not #> needed. Absolute fit of the Rasch model: RMSEA = 0.000 (close fit), CFI = #> 1.000, SRMSR = 0.022. autoplot(sel) Figure 3.1: Model comparison for LSAT6: each model’s information criterion relative to the best model (0 = best). The weight column converts BIC differences into the relative support for each model; here nearly all of it goes to the Rasch model. 3.3 Example 2: when the criteria disagree Now take the 32 science items of SAT12, scored with the corrected key from Chapter 1. # SAT12 science items, scored with the corrected key (item 32 keyed 3). key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,3) resp <- key2binary(SAT12, key) sel <- select_model(resp, verbose = FALSE) sel #> mirtverse model selection (ranked by BIC) #> #> model npar logLik AIC BIC SABIC RMSEA CFI delta weight #> 2PL 64 -9622 19373 19654 19451 0.029 0.953 0.0 1 #> Rasch 33 -9768 19602 19747 19642 0.039 0.905 92.5 0 #> 3PL 96 -9572 19337 19759 19454 0.022 0.975 104.5 0 #> #> The 2PL model is recommended because it has the lowest BIC (19654.2). The #> runner-up, Rasch, is 92.5 BIC points worse, which is very strong evidence for #> the 2PL model. Likelihood-ratio test Rasch vs. 2PL: chi-square(31) = 290.83, p #> < .001; the 2PL model fits significantly better. Likelihood-ratio test 2PL vs. #> 3PL: chi-square(32) = 100.16, p < .001; the 3PL model fits significantly #> better. Note the tension: the likelihood-ratio test prefers 3PL, while BIC #> penalizes extra parameters and prefers 2PL. Choose 2PL if parsimony matters #> most, or 3PL if fit to these data matters most. AIC would instead select the #> 3PL model. Absolute fit of the 2PL model: RMSEA = 0.029 (close fit), CFI = #> 0.953, SRMSR = 0.045. sel$lrt #> # A tibble: 3 × 5 #> simpler complex X2 df p.value #> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <int> <dbl> #> 1 Rasch 2PL 291. 31 5.30e-44 #> 2 Rasch 3PL 391. 63 7.62e-49 #> 3 2PL 3PL 100. 32 6.00e- 9 This time the evidence is mixed. The LRT and AIC prefer the 3PL, while BIC prefers the 2PL. Neither is “wrong”: they answer different questions. The LRT asks whether the extra 32 guessing parameters improve fit beyond chance, and with 600 people the answer is yes. BIC asks which model is more likely to be the better description once we account for the cost of 32 more parameters, and it says the 2PL. A sensible report states the tension and the reason for the final choice: if scores will be used for decisions about low-scoring students, where guessing matters most, the 3PL may be worth its cost; for a short research scale, the 2PL is easier to defend. 3.3.1 Small samples and convergence The 3PL is the hardest of the three to estimate, because the lower asymptote is determined only by what low-ability people do. With 200 students the EM algorithm may not converge at all: set.seed(303) small <- resp[sample(nrow(resp), 200), ] fit_small <- mirt(small, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE) extract.mirt(fit_small, "converged") #> [1] FALSE summary(coef(fit_small, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "g"]) #> Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. #> 0.000276 0.002136 0.079776 0.125231 0.207500 0.500034 Some lower asymptotes drift to zero and others to implausibly large values. Three common remedies are to use a 2PL, to fix \(c\) at a sensible value (for five-option items, 0.2), or to put a prior on \(c\) so that the data only move it away from a plausible value when they have something to say. In mirt a prior is part of the model syntax. Here a beta(5, 17) prior centres \(c\) near 0.2 (expbeta applies it on the scale mirt uses internally): spec <- mirt.model("F = 1-32 PRIOR = (1-32, g, expbeta, 5, 17)") fit_prior <- mirt(small, spec, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE) #> Warning: Observed log-likelihood may still be increasing. #> Final log-likelihood values were: #> -3154.689, -3151.159, -3149.755 extract.mirt(fit_prior, "converged") #> [1] TRUE summary(coef(fit_prior, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "g"]) #> Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. #> 0.109 0.181 0.192 0.187 0.195 0.235 With the prior the model converges and the lower asymptotes stay in a believable range. Report priors when you use them: they are part of the model. 3.4 Your turn For LSAT6, compute the LRT statistic for Rasch versus 2PL by hand from the two log-likelihoods, and check it against anova(). Fit the 2PL to SAT12 with quadpts = 15 and with the default of 61 points. Do the item parameters change? What does that tell you? Draw 300 students from SAT12 and rerun select_model(). Does the recommendation change? Repeat with another random sample. A colleague reports “the 3PL fitted significantly better (p < .001), so we used it”. What would you ask them? Solutions ll <- c(extract.mirt(rasch, "logLik"), extract.mirt(twopl, "logLik")) lrt <- 2 * (ll[2] - ll[1]) c(X2 = lrt, df = 4, p = pchisq(lrt, 4, lower.tail = FALSE)) #> X2 df p #> 0.569 4.000 0.966 m15 <- mirt(resp, 1, "2PL", quadpts = 15, verbose = FALSE) m61 <- mirt(resp, 1, "2PL", quadpts = 61, verbose = FALSE) max(abs(coef(m15, simplify = TRUE)$items - coef(m61, simplify = TRUE)$items)) #> [1] 0.142 With only 15 points some estimates move by about 0.1 on the slope-intercept scale; between 61 (the default for one dimension) and more points they hardly move at all. Fewer points trade accuracy for speed, which matters mainly for models with several dimensions. With fewer people, BIC’s penalty matters relatively more and the likelihood gains of the 3PL are smaller, so the 2PL (or even the Rasch model) is chosen more often. Model choice depends on the sample, not only on the items. Did the model converge? What did BIC say? How large is the sample? Are the guessing estimates plausible, and what were their standard errors? Would the scores or decisions differ between the 2PL and the 3PL? Chapter 4 Dimensionality and local independence Learning goals. After this chapter you can explain the assumptions of unidimensionality and local independence; compare one- and two-factor models and read rotated factor loadings; fit a confirmatory model in which each item measures a named dimension; read standardized residuals and Yen’s Q3, and tell local dependence from a second trait; choose a remedy for locally dependent items. Key terms: dimensionality, local independence, local dependence, Q3, multidimensional IRT. 4.1 The ideas The models in Chapter 2 make two related assumptions. Unidimensionality says that one latent trait accounts for the relationships among the items. Local independence says that once we know a person’s \(\theta\), their responses to different items are independent: the only reason two items correlate is that both depend on \(\theta\). Both can fail, in different ways. A test may measure two or more traits, for example reading and arithmetic in a set of mathematics word problems. Then a one-factor model forces two traits into one score, and the items of the smaller dimension look poorly discriminating. A small cluster of items may share something beyond the trait: a common reading passage, a shared stimulus, near-identical wording, or an item whose answer gives away the next. These pairs or clusters are locally dependent. They look like extra-good items, they inflate reliability, and they distort the item parameters. The tools differ too. For the first problem we compare models with one and two factors and look at the factor loadings. For the second we look at what is left over after fitting a one-factor model: if local independence holds, the residual correlations between item pairs should be close to zero. Yen’s Q3 statistic (Yen 1984) is the correlation between two items’ residuals. Values well above the average Q3 (often by 0.2 or more) flag dependent pairs. 4.2 Example 1: a mathematics test with a reading dimension We simulate a 24-item mathematics test taken by 1,500 Grade 8 students. Items M01 to M12 are calculation items. Items W01 to W12 are word problems that also depend on reading, which correlates 0.5 with calculation skill. # Simulated 24-item test, two correlated traits (r = 0.5), 12 items each. set.seed(404) a <- cbind(c(runif(12, 1.0, 2.0), runif(12, 0.3, 0.6)), c(rep(0, 12), runif(12, 1.0, 1.8))) d <- matrix(rnorm(24, 0, 0.8)) sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), 2) resp <- simdata(a, d, N = 1500, itemtype = "2PL", sigma = sigma) colnames(resp) <- c(sprintf("M%02d", 1:12), sprintf("W%02d", 1:12)) First, an exploratory comparison of one and two factors. We keep a copy of the data as math for the exercises. math <- resp f1 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) f2 <- mirt(resp, 2, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) anova(f1, f2) #> AIC SABIC HQ BIC logLik X2 df p #> f1 41008 41111 41103 41263 -20456 #> f2 40185 40337 40326 40563 -20022 868.777 23 0 The two-factor model is far better on every criterion. summary() shows the standardized loadings after an oblique rotation, which lets the factors correlate: summary(f2, rotate = "oblimin", suppress = 0.25) #> #> Rotation: oblimin #> #> Rotated factor loadings: #> #> F1 F2 h2 #> M01 0.708 0.509 #> M02 0.717 0.504 #> M03 0.663 0.453 #> M04 0.628 0.453 #> M05 0.581 0.360 #> M06 0.598 0.394 #> M07 0.665 0.398 #> M08 0.559 0.281 #> M09 0.473 0.233 #> M10 0.617 0.390 #> M11 0.715 0.539 #> M12 0.724 0.492 #> W01 0.634 0.428 #> W02 0.520 0.430 #> W03 0.751 0.572 #> W04 0.646 0.444 #> W05 0.588 0.373 #> W06 0.737 0.512 #> W07 0.560 0.451 #> W08 0.785 0.600 #> W09 0.697 0.484 #> W10 0.766 0.570 #> W11 0.775 0.555 #> W12 0.716 0.486 #> #> Rotated SS loadings: 5.67 5 #> #> Factor correlations: #> #> F1 F2 #> F1 1.000 #> F2 0.654 1 The calculation items load on one factor and the word problems on the other. The factor correlation is higher than the 0.5 we simulated between the two traits, because the word problems also need calculation skill: the rotation cannot separate that shared part cleanly, so some of it shows up as correlation between the factors. The one-factor fit statistics give the same message from the other side: rbind(one_factor = glance(f1)[, c("RMSEA", "SRMSR", "CFI")], two_factor = glance(f2)[, c("RMSEA", "SRMSR", "CFI")]) #> # A tibble: 2 × 3 #> RMSEA SRMSR CFI #> * <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 0.0644 0.0518 0.936 #> 2 0 0.0173 1 Exploratory models are useful for finding structure. When the structure is known from the test blueprint, a confirmatory model states it directly. Each item loads only on its own factor, and the factor correlation is estimated (COV = F1*F2): spec <- mirt.model("Calc = 1-12 Reading = 13-24 COV = Calc*Reading") cfa <- mirt(resp, spec, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) coef(cfa, simplify = TRUE)$cov #> Calc Reading #> Calc 1.000 0.676 #> Reading 0.676 1.000 anova(cfa, f2) #> AIC SABIC HQ BIC logLik X2 df p #> cfa 40174 40279 40271 40434 -20038 #> f2 40185 40337 40326 40563 -20022 32.658 22 0.067 The confirmatory model is nearly as good as the exploratory one with far fewer parameters, so BIC prefers it. What should we report to the school? That depends on use. Two subscores are defensible if each is reliable enough (Chapter 6); a single total score mixes two skills, and students with weak reading will look weaker at mathematics than they are. 4.3 Example 2: a reading passage that ties four items together In this test of 20 items, items R05 to R08 all refer to the same passage. Students who happen to understand the passage well do better on all four than their general reading ability predicts. We simulate this with a small extra factor that only those four items share. # Simulated 20-item reading test; R05-R08 share a passage (testlet effect). set.seed(405) a_gen <- runif(20, 1.0, 1.8) a_pas <- c(rep(0, 4), rep(2.0, 4), rep(0, 12)) resp <- simdata(cbind(a_gen, a_pas), matrix(rnorm(20, 0, 0.7)), N = 1200, itemtype = "2PL") colnames(resp) <- sprintf("R%02d", 1:20) We fit an ordinary unidimensional 2PL, as an analyst who did not know about the passage would, and look at the Q3 matrix. uni <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) gg_q3(uni) Figure 4.1: Q3 residual correlations from a unidimensional 2PL fitted to the reading test with a four-item passage. The six pairs among R05 to R08 stand out. Most other Q3 values are slightly negative, which is normal: residuals are a little negatively correlated on average, so we judge a pair against the average Q3 rather than against zero. The numbers behind the plot: q3 <- residuals(uni, type = "Q3", verbose = FALSE) round(q3[5:8, 5:8], 2) #> R05 R06 R07 R08 #> R05 1.00 0.31 0.25 0.28 #> R06 0.31 1.00 0.28 0.26 #> R07 0.25 0.28 1.00 0.24 #> R08 0.28 0.26 0.24 1.00 Local dependence has a cost. The unidimensional model has nowhere to put the passage effect, so it bends the item parameters to accommodate it and treats part of the passage effect as reading ability. Remedy 1 below shows how different the passage items look once the dependence is modelled. There are three common remedies. Model the dependence. A testlet or bifactor model gives the passage items a specific factor of their own, uncorrelated with the general factor. bfactor() fits it; its second argument says which specific factor each item belongs to (NA for none). specific <- c(rep(NA, 4), rep(1, 4), rep(NA, 12)) bf <- bfactor(resp, specific, verbose = FALSE) anova(uni, bf) #> AIC SABIC HQ BIC logLik X2 df p #> uni 28458 28534 28534 28661 -14189 #> bf 27901 27985 27985 28125 -13906 564.869 4 0 round(coef(bf, simplify = TRUE)$items[3:10, c("a1", "a2")], 2) #> a1 a2 #> R03 1.51 0.00 #> R04 0.93 0.00 #> R05 1.44 2.11 #> R06 1.45 2.20 #> R07 1.27 1.76 #> R08 1.88 1.99 #> R09 1.38 0.00 #> R10 1.31 0.00 The passage effect now has its own slope (a2), and the general slopes (a1) of R05 to R08 are higher than in the unidimensional model, which had diluted them. Compare them with coef(uni, simplify = TRUE)$items[5:8, "a1"]. Likelihood-ratio test and BIC both favour the bifactor model. Combine the items. Sum R05 to R08 into one polytomous “super-item” scored 0 to 4 and fit a polytomous model (Chapter 8). This is simple and robust, at the cost of some information. Drop or rewrite items in a future form, so that no two items depend on each other beyond the trait. 4.4 Your turn In Example 1, compute the sum score of the word problems and of the calculation items separately. How strongly do they correlate? Why is this lower than the factor correlation? Use select_model(resp, dims = 1:2) on the data of Example 1. Which model does it choose? Chapter 5 Item fit, person fit and item quality Learning goals. After this chapter you can explain what item fit means and why it is always fit to a model; compute and read the S-X² item-fit statistic and its RMSEA; compare an empirical item curve with the model curve; flag aberrant response patterns with the Zh person-fit statistic, and say what can cause them; summarize an item’s health for a review meeting. Key terms: item fit, S-X², empirical item curve, person fit, Zh, model fit. 5.1 The ideas Chapter 3 asked whether a model fits the test as a whole. Item fit asks the same question one item at a time: does the item’s curve describe how people at different ability levels actually responded? The most widely used statistic is Orlando and Thissen’s S-X² (Orlando and Thissen 2000). It groups people by their sum score, compares the observed proportion correct in each group with the proportion the model predicts, and adds up the squared differences. A small p-value means the item does not follow the model. Because a test has many items, some will be flagged by chance, so it is good practice to adjust the p-values (for example with the Benjamini-Hochberg method) and to look at an effect size too: mirt reports an RMSEA for each item, where values below about 0.05 mean the misfit is small in practice. Item fit is always fit to a particular model. An item with an unusually steep curve fits the 2PL perfectly well but misfits the Rasch model, which forces all slopes to be equal. A misfitting item is a question, not a verdict: look at the empirical curve, the content and the key before you decide. Person fit turns the question around: does a person’s response pattern look like what the model expects of someone at their \(\theta\)? The Zh statistic (Drasgow et al. 1985) is a standardized log-likelihood of the pattern. Values near zero are typical; large negative values (below about -2) mean the pattern is unlikely: a strong student who misses easy items, or a weak one who gets the hardest items right. Causes include careless responding, guessing, cheating, misaligned answer sheets, fatigue and atypical instruction. Zh flags a pattern for a closer look; it never proves misconduct. 5.2 Example 1: the same items under two models We return to the SAT12 science items, scored with the corrected key. # SAT12 science items, scored with the corrected key (item 32 keyed 3). key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,3) resp <- key2binary(SAT12, key) First, the Rasch model. gg_itemfit() plots each item’s S-X² RMSEA and marks the items whose p-value is below alpha. rasch <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE) gg_itemfit(rasch, p_adjust = "BH") Figure 5.1: S-\(X^2\) RMSEA of each SAT12 item under the Rasch model; flagged items are marked. item_table() puts the classical statistics, IRT parameters, fit and flags in one table. Here are the items that misfit the Rasch model most: tab_r <- item_table(rasch, p_adjust = "BH") tab_r[order(tab_r$p.value), c("item", "item_total_r", "location", "S_X2", "df", "RMSEA", "p.value")][1:5, ] #> # A tibble: 5 × 7 #> item item_total_r location S_X2 df RMSEA p.value #> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 Item.12 0.0685 0.394 91.7 18 0.0827 2.26e-10 #> 2 Item.30 0.157 0.274 60.7 18 0.0629 2.52e- 5 #> 3 Item.4 0.236 0.574 53.1 18 0.0571 2.69e- 4 #> 4 Item.31 0.425 -1.85 41.3 17 0.0488 6.80e- 3 #> 5 Item.32 0.203 0.258 41.4 18 0.0466 8.45e- 3 The worst-fitting items include items whose item-total correlation is far from the typical value: either much flatter or much steeper than the common slope the Rasch model imposes. Now fit the 2PL, which lets the slopes vary: twopl <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) tab_2 <- item_table(twopl, p_adjust = "BH") c(misfit_rasch = sum(tab_r$p.value < 0.01), misfit_2pl = sum(tab_2$p.value < 0.01)) #> misfit_rasch misfit_2pl #> 5 0 The 2PL removes the misfit. Whether that is the right response depends on the purpose. A Rasch programme would rather revise or drop the items that do not fit, because equal slopes give the sum score its simple meaning; a 2PL programme would keep them. An empirical item curve shows the misfit directly. People are grouped by their estimated \(\theta\), and the observed proportion correct in each group is plotted against the model curve: worst <- tab_r$item[which.min(tab_r$p.value)] gg_empirical(rasch, worst) + gg_empirical(twopl, worst) Figure 5.2: Empirical item curve of the worst-fitting item under the Rasch model (left) and the 2PL (right). Under the Rasch model the observed points do not follow the curve; under the 2PL they do. Fit is not the only thing that matters about an item, though. item_table() also flags items that are very easy or very hard, or that discriminate poorly: tab_2[tab_2$flag != "", c("item", "mean", "item_total_r", "discrimination", "location", "flag")] #> # A tibble: 7 × 6 #> item mean item_total_r discrimination location flag #> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr> #> 1 Item.9 0.885 0.123 0.518 -4.13 extreme location; low item… #> 2 Item.11 0.983 0.150 1.69 -3.07 extreme location; low item… #> 3 Item.12 0.415 0.0685 0.156 2.21 low discrimination; low it… #> 4 Item.17 0.963 0.199 1.53 -2.71 low item-total correlation #> 5 Item.21 0.915 0.131 0.600 -4.19 extreme location; low item… #> 6 Item.30 0.44 0.157 0.383 0.647 low discrimination; low it… #> 7 Item.32 0.443 0.203 0.490 0.484 low discrimination An item health card collects everything about one item on a page, with a traffic-light status, for item review meetings: weak <- tab_2$item[which.min(tab_2$discrimination)] item_card(twopl, weak) Figure 5.3: Item health card of the SAT12 item with the lowest discrimination under the 2PL. item_cards(twopl, file = "cards.html") writes a card for every item into one HTML page that reviewers can open in a browser. 5.3 Example 2: finding aberrant response patterns We simulate a 30-item quiz taken by 1,000 students. Most students respond according to a 2PL model, but 40 answered at random (careless responding) and 30 weak students somehow got the ten hardest items right (perhaps they saw them in advance). We record who is who so we can check the person-fit statistic. # Simulated 30-item quiz: 930 regular students, 40 random responders and # 30 weak students who know the 10 hardest items. `type` records which. set.seed(505) a <- matrix(rlnorm(30, 0.2, 0.2)); b <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 30) resp <- simdata(a, matrix(-a * b), N = 1000, itemtype = "2PL") colnames(resp) <- sprintf("Q%02d", 1:30) type <- rep(c("regular", "random", "preknowledge"), c(930, 40, 30)) resp[type == "random", ] <- rbinom(40 * 30, 1, 0.5) weak <- simdata(a, matrix(-a * b), N = 30, itemtype = "2PL", Theta = matrix(rnorm(30, -1.2, 0.3))) weak[, 21:30] <- 1 resp[type == "preknowledge", ] <- weak augment() adds each person’s score, its standard error and, with person_fit = TRUE, the Zh statistic to the data: mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) scores <- augment(mod, person_fit = TRUE) scores$type <- type head(scores[, c(".F1", ".se_F1", ".Zh", "type")]) #> # A tibble: 6 × 4 #> .F1 .se_F1 .Zh type #> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr> #> 1 -1.74 0.472 0.166 regular #> 2 1.48 0.406 0.970 regular #> 3 -0.422 0.388 0.809 regular #> 4 -0.0768 0.376 -0.238 regular #> 5 1.01 0.380 1.03 regular #> 6 -0.822 0.407 -0.218 regular How well does Zh separate the groups? library(ggplot2) ggplot(scores, aes(.Zh, fill = type)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, position = "identity", alpha = 0.6) + geom_vline(xintercept = -2, linetype = 2) + labs(x = "Zh person-fit statistic", y = "Students", fill = NULL) + theme_mirtverse() Figure 5.4: Distribution of the Zh person-fit statistic for regular students, random responders and students with pre-knowledge. aggregate(.Zh < -2 ~ type, data = scores, FUN = mean) #> type .Zh < -2 #> 1 preknowledge 1.00000 #> 2 random 0.85000 #> 3 regular 0.00323 All of the students with pre-knowledge are flagged: getting the hardest items right while missing easier ones is very unlikely under the model. Most random responders are flagged too, because on a 30-item test with a wide range of difficulties a coin-flip pattern contradicts the model again and again. Only a handful of regular students fall below -2. Real data are rarely this clean: aberrance is usually milder, and only part of a test may be affected (the last items, say, for a student who ran out of time). That is why Zh is a screening tool: flagged patterns need a human look, and often other evidence such as response times (see the response-time article). Do the aberrant patterns distort the item parameters? We can check by refitting without the flagged students and comparing both sets of difficulties for the ten hardest items with the values used to simulate the data: clean <- mirt(resp[scores$.Zh >= -2, ], 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) b_all <- coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[21:30, "b"] b_clean <- coef(clean, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[21:30, "b"] round(c(error_all = mean(abs(b_all - b[21:30])), error_clean = mean(abs(b_clean - b[21:30]))), 3) #> error_all error_clean #> 0.145 0.140 Here the difference is small, because only 7% of the students are aberrant and the model is estimated from everyone else. With more contamination, or with pre-knowledge concentrated on a few items, the damage grows, and removing flagged cases before calibration is common practice. 5.4 Your turn Plot the empirical curve of the best-fitting item under the Rasch model in Example 1. With 32 tests, report the adjusted results, and look at the RMSEA to judge size. Chapter 6 Information, precision and reliability Learning goals. After this chapter you can read item and test information curves; convert information into a conditional standard error of measurement; compute marginal and empirical reliability, and explain why a single reliability coefficient hides how precision changes along the scale; use information to judge whether a test is well targeted for a decision. Key terms: item information, test information, standard error of measurement, marginal reliability, targeting, precision. 6.1 The ideas In classical test theory a test has one standard error of measurement for everyone. In IRT, precision depends on where you are on the scale. An item tells us most about people whose ability is close to its difficulty: for them the outcome is most uncertain, so observing it is most informative. The item information function of a 2PL item is \[I_j(\theta) = a_j^2 \, P_j(\theta)\,[1 - P_j(\theta)],\] which peaks at \(\theta = b_j\), where \(P_j = 0.5\), with height \(a_j^2/4\). A steep item gives a lot of information in a narrow range; a flat item a little information over a wide range. For the 3PL the peak is lower and a little above \(b_j\), because guessing makes correct answers less informative. Information adds up over items. The test information function is the sum of the item information functions, and the conditional standard error of a \(\theta\) estimate is approximately \[SE(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{I(\theta)}}.\] So doubling the information shrinks the standard error by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\), not 2. A test information of 10 gives \(SE \approx 0.32\), and on a scale with standard deviation 1 that corresponds to a reliability of about \(1 - 0.32^2 = 0.90\) for people at that point. Two summary reliability coefficients are common: Marginal reliability averages the error variance over the assumed population distribution of \(\theta\): \(\rho = 1 - \overline{SE^2}/\sigma^2_\theta\). Empirical reliability does the same with the estimated scores and their standard errors in the sample. Both are useful single numbers, but a test can have a respectable overall reliability and still be imprecise exactly where an important decision is made. That is why we look at the curves. 6.2 Example 1: where does the science test measure well? # SAT12 science items, scored with the corrected key (item 32 keyed 3). key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,3) resp <- key2binary(SAT12, key) mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) gg_info(mod) + gg_info(mod, type = "se") Figure 6.1: Test information (left) and standard error of measurement (right) for the SAT12 science test under the 2PL. The test is most informative a little below average ability and loses precision quickly above \(\theta = 1\). The values behind the curves: theta <- matrix(-3:3) data.frame(theta = theta[, 1], information = testinfo(mod, theta), se = 1 / sqrt(testinfo(mod, theta))) #> theta information se #> 1 -3 3.53 0.533 #> 2 -2 5.82 0.415 #> 3 -1 7.12 0.375 #> 4 0 5.74 0.417 #> 5 1 4.12 0.492 #> 6 2 2.41 0.644 #> 7 3 1.31 0.875 Each item’s contribution: gg_info(mod, type = "items", which.items = c(1, 6, 9, 12, 19, 28)) Figure 6.2: Item information curves of six SAT12 items. Items differ a lot. Steep items in the middle of the scale do most of the work; very easy items (such as Item.9) add information only far below average, and flat items (such as Item.12) add almost nothing anywhere. Reliability: marginal_rxx(mod) #> [1] 0.837 empirical_rxx(fscores(mod, full.scores.SE = TRUE)) #> F1 #> 0.838 areainfo() tells us how much of the test’s total information lies in a range of the scale, here between \(\theta = -1\) and \(\theta = 1\): areainfo(mod, c(-1, 1)) #> LowerBound UpperBound Info TotalInfo Proportion nitems #> -1 1 11.4 34.2 0.334 32 Suppose the school awards a science prize to students above \(\theta = 1.5\). At that point the standard error is 1 / sqrt(testinfo(mod, matrix(1.5))) #> [1] 0.559 about half a standard deviation. A student estimated at 1.5 could easily have a true ability of 1.0 or 2.0. The overall reliability of about 0.84 gives a much rosier picture than the precision at the decision point. 6.3 Example 2: designing a test for a decision Information curves are also a design tool. Imagine a calibrated pool of 90 2PL items for a nursing entrance test, with a pass mark at \(\theta = 0.5\). We compare three 20-item forms built from the pool, without collecting any new data: the information function only needs the item parameters. # A pool of 90 calibrated 2PL items (a, b), as stored in an item bank. # No responses are needed: this example works from item parameters only. set.seed(606) pool <- data.frame(item = sprintf("N%02d", 1:90), a = rlnorm(90, 0.15, 0.3), b = rnorm(90, -0.3, 1.1)) A small function computes 2PL information from the formula above: info_2pl <- function(items, theta) { sapply(theta, function(t) { p <- plogis(items$a * (t - items$b)) sum(items$a^2 * p * (1 - p)) }) } Three ways to choose 20 items: forms <- list( random = pool[sample(nrow(pool), 20), ], spread = pool[order(pool$b)[round(seq(1, 90, length.out = 20))], ], targeted = pool[order(abs(pool$b - 0.5) / pool$a)[1:20], ] ) grid <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.05) curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(forms), function(f) data.frame(form = f, theta = grid, info = info_2pl(forms[[f]], grid)))) library(ggplot2) ggplot(curves, aes(theta, info, colour = form)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = 2) + labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Test information", colour = "Form") + theme_mirtverse() Figure 6.3: Test information of three 20-item forms drawn from the nursing pool; the dashed line marks the pass mark. The targeted form picks items whose difficulty is close to the pass mark, favouring steep ones (dividing by \(a\) ranks steep items first). The spread form covers the whole range evenly, and the random form is what we get by chance. At the pass mark: sapply(forms, function(f) c(info = info_2pl(f, 0.5), se = 1 / sqrt(info_2pl(f, 0.5)))) #> random spread targeted #> info 4.17 5.879 10.44 #> se 0.49 0.412 0.31 The targeted form has more than twice as much information at the pass mark as the random one, with the same number of items. The price is precision far from the cut: the spread form is better for reporting scores across the whole range. Which is better depends on what the scores are for. A licensing test cares about the pass mark; a progress test cares about everyone. Chapter 11 builds on this idea with automated test assembly and adaptive testing. 6.4 Your turn Show, using info_2pl() and a single item with \(a = 2\), \(b = 0\), that the information peaks at \(\theta = 0\) with height \(a^2/4 = 1\). In Example 1, how many items like the average SAT12 item would you need to add to bring the standard error at \(\theta = 1.5\) down to 0.35? In Example 2, build a 30-item targeted form. How much does the standard error at the pass mark improve over the 20-item targeted form? Explain to a colleague why “the test has a reliability of 0.84” is not enough to decide whether it can be used to award the prize. Solutions one <- data.frame(a = 2, b = 0) grid[which.max(info_2pl(one, grid))]; max(info_2pl(one, grid)) #> [1] 0 #> [1] 1 # 2. information needed for SE = 0.35, and the average item information at 1.5 need <- 1 / 0.35^2 have <- testinfo(mod, matrix(1.5)) per_item <- have / 32 ceiling((need - have) / per_item) #> [1] 50 t30 <- pool[order(abs(pool$b - 0.5) / pool$a)[1:30], ] 1 / sqrt(c(twenty = info_2pl(forms$targeted, 0.5), thirty = info_2pl(t30, 0.5))) #> twenty thirty #> 0.310 0.272 Many more items, because the average item adds little information at 1.5. Adding a few hard, discriminating items would be far more efficient than adding average ones. Reliability is an average over everybody. The prize decision happens at \(\theta = 1.5\), where the test has much less information than in the middle; what matters is the standard error there. Chapter 7 Scoring people Learning goals. After this chapter you can compare EAP, MAP, ML and WLE scores and say when each is a sensible choice; explain why maximum likelihood fails for perfect and zero scores; convert sum scores to IRT scores with a conversion table; read a Wright map; estimate how often people are classified on the wrong side of a cut score. Key terms: person score, EAP, MAP, ML, WLE, Wright map, classification accuracy. 7.1 The ideas Once the item parameters are known, we can estimate each person’s \(\theta\) from their responses. The likelihood of a response pattern, viewed as a function of \(\theta\), is the product of the item probabilities: \(P_j(\theta)\) for each item answered correctly and \(1 - P_j(\theta)\) for each item answered wrongly. The four common estimators use it differently. ML (maximum likelihood) takes the \(\theta\) that maximizes the likelihood. It uses only the responses, which makes it attractive for fairness arguments, but it does not exist for all-correct or all-wrong patterns (the likelihood keeps rising towards \(\pm\infty\)), and it is biased outwards for short tests. WLE (weighted likelihood, Warm (1989)) adds a small correction that removes most of ML’s bias and gives finite estimates for perfect patterns. MAP (maximum a posteriori) multiplies the likelihood by a prior distribution for \(\theta\), usually the population distribution, and takes the mode of the result. EAP (expected a posteriori) takes the mean of that posterior. It is easy to compute, always finite and has the smallest average error, which is why it is mirt’s default. Like MAP, it shrinks estimates towards the population mean, more so when the test is short. The standard error of an EAP estimate is the standard deviation of the posterior, and it comes for free. For the Rasch model the sum score carries all the information about \(\theta\), so everyone with the same sum score gets the same estimate. For the 2PL and 3PL, two people with the same sum score can get different estimates, because correct answers to steep items count for more. Some programmes still want one score per sum score. EAP for sum scores (method = "EAPsum") gives exactly that, and produces a conversion table that can be printed in a manual. 7.2 Example 1: four estimators, one short test With only five items, the differences between estimators are easy to see. # Five dichotomous LSAT items, one row per test taker. resp <- expand.table(LSAT7) mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) patterns <- unique(resp) est <- sapply(c("EAP", "MAP", "ML", "WLE"), function(m) fscores(mod, method = m, response.pattern = patterns)[, "F1"]) scored <- data.frame(pattern = apply(patterns, 1, paste, collapse = ""), sum = rowSums(patterns), round(est, 2)) scored[order(scored$sum, scored$EAP), ][c(1:4, 15:18, 29:32), ] #> pattern sum EAP MAP ML WLE #> 1 00000 0 -1.87 -1.82 -Inf -4.14 #> 13 00001 1 -1.53 -1.49 -3.12 -2.60 #> 32 00010 1 -1.51 -1.48 -3.07 -2.56 #> 173 10000 1 -1.41 -1.39 -2.71 -2.31 #> 264 10100 2 -0.65 -0.69 -1.17 -1.15 #> 107 01100 2 -0.61 -0.65 -1.11 -1.10 #> 230 10011 3 -0.75 -0.78 -1.31 -1.26 #> 100 01011 3 -0.70 -0.74 -1.25 -1.21 #> 145 01111 4 0.14 0.06 0.13 -0.22 #> 525 11101 4 0.27 0.18 0.43 -0.03 #> 661 11110 4 0.28 0.20 0.47 -0.01 #> 693 11111 5 0.73 0.64 Inf 1.09 Read the table from top to bottom. For the all-wrong pattern ML gives -Inf, and for the all-correct pattern Inf; WLE, MAP and EAP give finite values. EAP and MAP are pulled towards zero compared with ML and WLE. And patterns with the same sum score get different scores under the 2PL, because Item.3 (the steepest) counts for more than Item.5. The province calls students at or above \(\theta = 0.8\) proficient. Because the data are simulated we know each student’s true \(\theta\), so we can see how often the estimates put students on the wrong side of the cut. # Simulated 40-item mathematics test; true_theta is known for checking. set.seed(707) true_theta <- rnorm(2000) a <- matrix(rlnorm(40, 0.1, 0.25)); b <- rnorm(40, 0, 1) resp <- simdata(a, matrix(-a * b), N = 2000, itemtype = "2PL", Theta = matrix(true_theta)) colnames(resp) <- sprintf("M%02d", 1:40) mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) eap <- fscores(mod, method = "EAP", full.scores.SE = TRUE) wle <- fscores(mod, method = "WLE", full.scores.SE = TRUE) #> Warning: The following factor score estimates failed to converge successfully: #> 1586 c(cor_eap = cor(eap[, 1], true_theta), cor_wle = cor(wle[, 1], true_theta), sd_eap = sd(eap[, 1]), sd_wle = sd(wle[, 1])) #> cor_eap cor_wle sd_eap sd_wle #> 0.945 0.945 0.947 1.049 With 40 items both estimators correlate about 0.95 with the true values, and they rank students almost identically. A student is classified correctly if the estimate and the true value fall on the same side of the cut. cut <- 0.8 truth <- true_theta >= cut observed <- eap[, 1] >= cut table(true = truth, estimated = observed) #> estimated #> true FALSE TRUE #> FALSE 1503 58 #> TRUE 81 358 mean(truth == observed) #> [1] 0.93 In practice we never know the truth, but we can estimate the accuracy from the scores and their standard errors (Rudner 2001). Chapter 8 Polytomous items and open-ended responses Learning goals. After this chapter you can fit the partial credit, generalized partial credit and graded response models, and say how they differ; read category response curves and thresholds; recognise disordered thresholds and decide whether to collapse categories; describe how rater-scored open-ended responses fit into an IRT analysis. Key terms: polytomous item, graded response model, GPCM, category response curve, threshold, expected score, QWK. 8.1 The ideas Many items have more than two score categories: rating scales (strongly disagree to strongly agree), partial-credit mathematics problems, essays scored 0 to 4 against a rubric. Three families of models are used most. The graded response model (GRM, Samejima (1969)) models the cumulative probability of scoring in category \(k\) or higher with a 2PL curve, \(P(X \ge k \mid \theta) = \text{logistic}[a(\theta - b_k)]\). The thresholds \(b_1 < b_2 < \dots\) are ordered by construction: \(b_k\) is where a person has a 50% chance of scoring \(k\) or more. The partial credit model (PCM, Masters (1982)) is the polytomous Rasch model. It models each step from category \(k-1\) to \(k\) as a Rasch item, with a step difficulty \(b_k\). All items share the same slope. The generalized partial credit model (GPCM, Muraki (1992)) adds an item slope to the PCM. In the PCM and GPCM the step difficulties are the points where adjacent category curves cross. They do not have to be in order. Disordered steps (for example \(b_2 < b_1\)) mean that a middle category is never the most likely response at any ability: respondents skip over it. That is often a sign of a category label that is unclear or a rubric level that raters cannot distinguish, and a common remedy is to merge the category with a neighbour. Each item’s expected score curve, the average score as a function of \(\theta\), summarizes the categories in one line and is often the easiest plot to explain. 8.2 Example 1: attitudes to science Science holds the responses of 392 people to four statements about science and technology, each rated on a four-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 4 = strongly agree). # Four 4-category attitude items (scored 1-4), 392 respondents. resp <- Science select_model() compares the three models: sel <- select_model(resp, verbose = FALSE) sel #> mirtverse model selection (ranked by BIC) #> #> model npar logLik AIC BIC SABIC RMSEA CFI delta weight #> GRM 16 -1609 3250 3313 3263 0.148 0.910 0.00 0.795 #> PCM (Rasch) 13 -1619 3265 3316 3275 0.117 0.860 2.90 0.187 #> GPCM 16 -1613 3257 3321 3270 0.136 0.924 7.63 0.018 #> #> The GRM model is recommended because it has the lowest BIC (3313.3). The #> runner-up, PCM (Rasch), is 2.9 BIC points worse, which is positive evidence for #> the GRM model. Absolute fit of the GRM model: RMSEA = 0.148 (poor fit), CFI = #> 0.910, SRMSR = 0.073. The GRM has the lowest BIC, but the absolute fit (RMSEA) is not good for any of the three. With only four items, M2 has few degrees of freedom and RMSEA is unstable, so read it with care, and look at the items. grm <- sel$models[["GRM"]] tidy(grm) #> # A tibble: 16 × 5 #> item itemtype term estimate std.error #> <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 Comfort graded a 1.04 NA #> 2 Comfort graded b1 -4.67 NA #> 3 Comfort graded b2 -2.53 NA #> 4 Comfort graded b3 1.41 NA #> 5 Work graded a 1.23 NA #> 6 Work graded b1 -2.39 NA #> 7 Work graded b2 -0.735 NA #> 8 Work graded b3 1.85 NA #> 9 Future graded a 2.29 NA #> 10 Future graded b1 -2.28 NA #> 11 Future graded b2 -0.965 NA #> 12 Future graded b3 0.856 NA #> 13 Benefit graded a 1.09 NA #> 14 Benefit graded b1 -3.06 NA #> 15 Benefit graded b2 -0.906 NA #> 16 Benefit graded b3 1.54 NA Each item has one slope and three thresholds. Future has by far the steepest slope. The category curves show how the thresholds divide the scale: gg_trace(grm) Figure 8.1: Category response curves of the graded response model for the four Science items. and the expected score curves summarize them: gg_trace(grm, type = "expected", facet = FALSE) Figure 8.2: Expected item score curves of the graded response model for the Science items. The lowest category is rare for every item: its first threshold is far below average, so the curve for “strongly disagree” only rises for people far out in the left tail. The Wright map shows every threshold next to the distribution of people: gg_wright(grm) Figure 8.3: Wright map of the Science items: category thresholds next to the distribution of people. 8.3 Example 2: a rating category nobody uses We simulate a six-item job satisfaction scale with five categories (0 to 4), answered by 1,500 employees. On item J3 the middle label was badly worded, so respondents tend to skip category 2. # Simulated 6-item, 5-category scale; item J3 has disordered steps. set.seed(808) steps <- rbind(c(-2.0, -0.8, 0.4, 1.6), c(-1.8, -0.6, 0.6, 1.8), c(-1.6, 0.9, -0.3, 1.4), # J3: step 2 harder than step 3 c(-2.2, -1.0, 0.2, 1.4), c(-1.9, -0.7, 0.5, 1.7), c(-1.7, -0.5, 0.7, 1.9)) a <- c(1.3, 1.5, 1.4, 1.2, 1.6, 1.3) d <- cbind(0, -a * t(apply(steps, 1, cumsum))) # GPCM intercepts resp <- simdata(matrix(a), d, N = 1500, itemtype = "gpcm") colnames(resp) <- paste0("J", 1:6) The category frequencies already hint at the problem: round(t(apply(resp, 2, function(x) table(factor(x, levels = 0:4)) / length(x))), 2) #> 0 1 2 3 4 #> J1 0.05 0.21 0.34 0.28 0.12 #> J2 0.07 0.23 0.37 0.24 0.08 #> J3 0.12 0.41 0.10 0.25 0.13 #> J4 0.05 0.18 0.32 0.30 0.14 #> J5 0.07 0.22 0.36 0.27 0.08 #> J6 0.09 0.24 0.37 0.22 0.08 Fit the GPCM and look at the step parameters: gpcm <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "gpcm", verbose = FALSE) coef(gpcm, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items #> a b1 b2 b3 b4 #> J1 1.33 -2.14 -0.831 0.345 1.53 #> J2 1.51 -1.87 -0.665 0.603 1.72 #> J3 1.24 -1.81 1.008 -0.380 1.44 #> J4 1.18 -2.20 -0.963 0.163 1.39 #> J5 1.46 -1.92 -0.723 0.501 1.76 #> J6 1.21 -1.75 -0.625 0.768 1.87 For J3 the second step (\(b_2\)) is larger than the third (\(b_3\)), unlike every other item. The category curves make it plain: category 2 of J3 is never the most likely response. gg_trace(gpcm, which.items = c("J2", "J3")) Figure 8.4: Category response curves of J2 and J3; category 2 of J3 is never the most likely response. Disordered steps are not always a problem; they mean a category is rarely the most likely response, not that nobody uses it. Look at the wording or the rubric, and at how many people chose the category. Here we decide that the middle label is unclear and merge categories 1 and 2 of J3, so it is scored 0 to 3: collapsed <- resp collapsed[, "J3"] <- c(0, 1, 1, 2, 3)[resp[, "J3"] + 1] gpcm_c <- mirt(collapsed, 1, itemtype = "gpcm", verbose = FALSE) coef(gpcm_c, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items["J3", ] #> a b1 b2 b3 b4 #> 1.613 -1.663 0.575 1.302 NA The steps of the collapsed item are now in order. The GRM would never have shown the problem, because its thresholds are ordered by definition: this is one reason to fit a PCM or GPCM when you are developing a rating scale. 8.4 Open-ended responses and raters Open-ended tasks, such as essays and constructed responses, are usually scored by trained raters against a rubric, and then analysed with a polytomous model like the ones above. Two extra questions come first. Do the raters agree? Agreement on ordinal scores is usually summarized by exact agreement and by quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), which gives partial credit for near misses (Cohen 1968). Are some raters harsher or less consistent than others? Rater effects can be studied by comparing each rater’s scores with those of the other raters on the same responses, or with models that include rater parameters. mirtverse’s assessment pipeline has a scoring stage for this, score_open(), which resolves two reads into a final score and checks agreement (see section 9 of the assessment pipeline article). Lab 6 works through the whole process with eight raters and an automated scoring engine. 8.5 Your turn Fit the PCM (itemtype = "Rasch") to Science. Are any of its step difficulties disordered? In Example 2, fit the GRM to the original data. What do the thresholds of J3 look like, and why do they not reveal the problem? Compare the test information of the original and the collapsed GPCM. How much information is lost by collapsing one category of one item? Two raters score 200 essays from 0 to 4 and agree exactly on 60% of them. Why is QWK a better summary than exact agreement for deciding whether the raters can be trusted? Solutions pcm <- mirt(Science, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE) coef(pcm, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items #> a b1 b2 b3 #> Comfort 1 -3.09 -2.595 1.39 #> Work 1 -1.90 -0.911 1.86 #> Future 1 -2.65 -1.421 1.14 #> Benefit 1 -2.45 -0.900 1.36 grm2 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE) coef(grm2, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items["J3", ] #> a b1 b2 b3 b4 #> 1.9899 -1.6164 0.0767 0.4230 1.5352 theta <- matrix(seq(-3, 3, by = 1)) round(rbind(original = testinfo(gpcm, theta), collapsed = testinfo(gpcm_c, theta)), 2) #> [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7] #> original 1.95 4.19 5.80 6.99 6.16 3.64 1.43 #> collapsed 1.95 4.41 5.89 6.31 6.34 3.85 1.42 The GRM thresholds of J3 are in order, because the model forces them to be; the second and third are just close together. Hardly any. At some points the collapsed model even has a little more information, because the slope of J3 is estimated higher once the model no longer has to accommodate the skipped category. Collapsing a category that people skip costs almost nothing. Exact agreement treats a 3 versus 4 disagreement the same as a 0 versus 4 disagreement. QWK weights disagreements by their size and corrects for agreement by chance, so it reflects whether the raters rank the essays in the same way.
