Chapter 9 Differential item functioning and fairness Learning goals. After this chapter you can tell impact (a real difference between groups) from DIF (an item that works differently for people of the same ability); run an IRT likelihood-ratio DIF analysis and read its effect sizes; distinguish uniform from non-uniform DIF; run a Mantel-Haenszel DIF test and classify items with the ETS A/B/C rules; explain why anchor items matter. Key terms: DIF, reference and focal groups, uniform and non-uniform DIF, DIF effect size, anchor items. 9.1 The ideas Groups often differ in their average scores. That alone says nothing about whether a test is fair: the groups may simply differ in what the test measures, which is called impact. An item shows differential item functioning (DIF) when people from different groups with the same ability have different chances of answering it correctly (Holland and Wainer 1993). DIF is a statistical finding, not a verdict of bias; a content review decides whether the reason is irrelevant to what the test should measure (bias) or a real difference in what was taught. We compare a reference group (often the majority group) with a focal group. In IRT terms, DIF means the item has different parameters in the two groups. Uniform DIF: the item is harder for one group at every ability level (the difficulty differs, the curves are parallel). Non-uniform DIF: the size or direction of the difference changes with ability (the slopes differ and the curves cross). To compare groups we must first put them on a common scale, and that needs items we trust to work the same way in both: the anchors. mirtverse’s dif() uses a constrained-baseline approach: it fits a multiple-group model in which all item parameters are equal across groups while the group means and variances are free, then frees each item’s parameters in turn and tests the change with a likelihood-ratio test. Items you do not test serve as anchors. Because each test involves only one free item, the approach works well when DIF is confined to a few items; when many items have DIF, a purification step (testing, removing flagged items from the anchor set, and testing again) is safer. A significant test is not enough: with large samples tiny differences are significant. dif() therefore reports effect sizes on the item score scale. The signed version (esd) is the average difference in the probability of a correct answer between the focal and the reference group at the same ability; the unsigned version (uesd) also captures crossing curves. The Mantel-Haenszel (MH) procedure (Holland and Thayer 1988) is the classical alternative. It matches people on their sum score, builds a 2 × 2 table (group × right/wrong) at every score level and tests whether the odds of a correct answer differ between groups across the tables. ETS classifies the size of MH DIF as A (negligible), B (moderate) or C (large). 9.2 Example 1: paper versus tablet A district moved its Grade 5 reading test from paper to tablets. We simulate 25 items answered by 1,200 students on paper (reference) and 800 on tablets (focal). The tablet group is slightly weaker on average (impact). Two items that ask students to drag text into a table are harder on tablets (uniform DIF), and one long-passage item is easier for strong tablet readers and harder for weak ones (non-uniform DIF). # Simulated 25-item reading test; `group` is the test mode for each student. set.seed(909) a <- matrix(rlnorm(25, 0.2, 0.25)); d <- matrix(rnorm(25, 0.2, 0.9)) a_tab <- a; d_tab <- d d_tab[c(7, 18)] <- d[c(7, 18)] - 0.8 # R07, R18: uniform DIF a_tab[22] <- a[22] * 1.8; d_tab[22] <- d[22] # R22: non-uniform DIF paper <- simdata(a, d, N = 1200, itemtype = "2PL") tablet <- simdata(a_tab, d_tab, N = 800, itemtype = "2PL", Theta = matrix(rnorm(800, -0.2, 1))) resp <- rbind(paper, tablet) colnames(resp) <- sprintf("R%02d", 1:25) group <- factor(rep(c("Paper", "Tablet"), c(1200, 800)), levels = c("Paper", "Tablet")) The raw scores differ between the groups, but that alone does not tell us which items, if any, are unfair: mode_resp <- resp; mode_group <- group # kept for the exercises tapply(rowSums(resp), group, mean) #> Paper Tablet #> 12.6 11.1 dif() tests every item. Paper is the reference group because it is the first level of the factor. res <- dif(resp, group = group) res #> DIF analysis: Paper (reference) vs Tablet; 25 items tested #> Likelihood-ratio tests freeing a1, d; BH-adjusted p < 0.05 flags DIF #> #> item X2 df p.value p.adjusted flag esd uesd converged #> R01 1.273 2 .529 .758 -0.007 0.018 TRUE #> R02 2.153 2 .341 .758 0.016 0.022 TRUE #> R03 0.264 2 .876 .876 0.005 0.009 TRUE #> R04 1.480 2 .477 .758 -0.022 0.022 TRUE #> R05 1.158 2 .560 .758 0.011 0.019 TRUE #> R06 0.953 2 .621 .758 -0.017 0.018 TRUE #> R07 29.459 2 < .001 < .001 DIF -0.100 0.100 TRUE #> R08 1.447 2 .485 .758 0.021 0.024 TRUE #> R09 1.793 2 .408 .758 -0.019 0.021 TRUE #> R10 5.327 2 .070 .290 0.013 0.044 TRUE #> R11 4.878 2 .087 .312 0.041 0.041 TRUE #> R12 7.665 2 .022 .108 0.041 0.047 TRUE #> R13 0.720 2 .698 .758 0.001 0.014 TRUE #> R14 1.044 2 .593 .758 0.018 0.018 TRUE #> R15 0.578 2 .749 .780 -0.007 0.012 TRUE #> R16 0.783 2 .676 .758 -0.011 0.013 TRUE #> R17 9.572 2 .008 .052 0.061 0.061 TRUE #> R18 45.538 2 < .001 < .001 DIF -0.135 0.135 TRUE #> R19 2.351 2 .309 .758 0.017 0.024 TRUE #> R20 1.087 2 .581 .758 -0.006 0.018 TRUE #> R21 1.270 2 .530 .758 0.002 0.019 TRUE #> R22 32.166 2 < .001 < .001 DIF 0.043 0.075 TRUE #> R23 4.298 2 .117 .364 0.028 0.032 TRUE #> R24 0.878 2 .645 .758 0.012 0.015 TRUE #> R25 1.456 2 .483 .758 0.024 0.024 TRUE The flagged items are the three we planted. Here, as a check, we test only the three flagged items against the other 22: dif(resp, group = group, items = c("R07", "R18", "R22"))$table #> # A tibble: 3 × 9 #> item X2 df p.value p.adjusted flag esd uesd converged #> <chr> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <lgl> <dbl> <dbl> <lgl> #> 1 R07 29.5 2 4.01e- 7 4.01e- 7 TRUE -0.0997 0.0997 TRUE #> 2 R18 45.5 2 1.29e-10 3.88e-10 TRUE -0.135 0.135 TRUE #> 3 R22 32.2 2 1.04e- 7 1.55e- 7 TRUE 0.0430 0.0755 TRUE Does the DIF matter for scores? One way to judge is to compare the expected total score of the test in the two groups at the same ability, which is called differential test functioning. With two items that are harder for tablet users and one that crosses, the total effect is a fraction of a score point; a content review would still look at the drag-and-drop items, because the problem can be fixed by changing the interface. 9.3 Example 2: Mantel-Haenszel on a chemistry quiz The MH test needs no IRT model, which makes it a good first screen and a useful check. We simulate a 20-item chemistry quiz taken by 600 girls and 600 boys of equal average ability; item C11 involves a sports context and is easier for boys of the same ability. # Simulated 20-item quiz; `group` is gender. C11 has uniform DIF. set.seed(910) a <- matrix(rlnorm(20, 0.2, 0.2)); d <- matrix(rnorm(20, 0, 0.8)) d_boys <- d; d_boys[11] <- d[11] + 0.7 resp <- rbind(simdata(a, d, N = 600, itemtype = "2PL"), simdata(a, d_boys, N = 600, itemtype = "2PL")) colnames(resp) <- sprintf("C%02d", 1:20) group <- factor(rep(c("Girl", "Boy"), each = 600), levels = c("Girl", "Boy")) For each item we match on the total score of the other items, build the stratified 2 × 2 tables and run the MH test. The common odds ratio \(\alpha_{MH}\) converts to the ETS delta scale as \(\text{MH D-DIF} = -2.35 \ln \alpha_{MH}\). The ETS rules call DIF negligible (A) when \(|\text{MH D-DIF}| < 1\) or the test is not significant, large (C) when \(|\text{MH D-DIF}| \ge 1.5\) and significant, and moderate (B) otherwise (the full rules also test the size against 1). mh_item <- function(resp, group, item) { rest <- rowSums(resp[, colnames(resp) != item]) strata <- cut(rest, unique(quantile(rest, 0:5 / 5)), include.lowest = TRUE) tab <- table(group, factor(resp[, item], levels = 1:0), strata) mh <- mantelhaen.test(tab, exact = FALSE) delta <- -2.35 * log(unname(mh$estimate)) data.frame(item = item, alpha_MH = unname(mh$estimate), MH_D_DIF = delta, p.value = mh$p.value, ETS = ifelse(mh$p.value >= 0.05 | abs(delta) < 1, "A", ifelse(abs(delta) >= 1.5, "C", "B"))) } mh <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(resp), mh_item, resp = resp, group = group)) mh[order(mh$p.value), ][1:5, ] #> item alpha_MH MH_D_DIF p.value ETS #> 11 C11 0.576 1.297 3.55e-05 B #> 4 C04 1.288 -0.596 4.54e-02 A #> 13 C13 0.789 0.556 1.22e-01 A #> 1 C01 1.222 -0.471 1.36e-01 A #> 9 C09 1.224 -0.476 1.42e-01 A The table is arranged so that \(\alpha_{MH}\) is the odds of a correct answer in the reference group (girls) divided by the odds in the focal group (boys), at the same score. Values above 1, and negative MH D-DIF, mean the item favours the reference group; values below 1, and positive MH D-DIF, favour the focal group. C11 stands out, with a moderate (B) DIF in favour of boys. Matching on five score bands keeps the tables reasonably full in a sample of this size; with more people you can match on every score. The IRT analysis agrees: subset(dif(resp, group = group)$table, flag) #> # A tibble: 1 × 9 #> item X2 df p.value p.adjusted flag esd uesd converged #> <chr> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <lgl> <dbl> <dbl> <lgl> #> 1 C11 18.1 2 0.000117 0.00233 TRUE 0.104 0.104 TRUE 9.4 Your turn In Example 1, refit dif() with p_adjust = "none". Chapter 10 Linking and equating Learning goals. After this chapter you can explain why two separately calibrated forms are not on the same scale; describe common-item (anchor) and common-person designs; link two calibrations with the mean-sigma and Stocking-Lord methods; check anchor items for parameter drift; run a concurrent calibration with a multiple-group model; carry a cut score from one form to another with IRT true-score equating. Key terms: linking, anchor items, moment linking, characteristic curve linking, parameter drift, test characteristic curve. 10.1 The ideas Every calibration fixes the scale by assuming that the people in it have \(\theta\) with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. If this year’s candidates are stronger than last year’s, a separate calibration of this year’s form will still put them at mean 0, and every item will look harder than it is. To compare forms, or groups, the two calibrations must be put on a common scale. That is linking; when the goal is to make scores on two forms interchangeable, it is called equating (Kolen and Brennan 2014). Because the IRT scale is only determined up to a linear transformation, linking amounts to finding two constants \(A\) and \(B\) such that, for the new form’s parameters, \[\theta^* = A\theta + B, \qquad b^* = A b + B, \qquad a^* = a / A.\] The constants come from information the two calibrations share. In the common design, the non-equivalent groups with anchor test (NEAT) design, the two forms share a set of anchor items. Two families of methods estimate \(A\) and \(B\) from the anchors. Moment methods. Mean-sigma matches the mean and standard deviation of the anchor difficulties: \(A = s_{b,\text{old}} / s_{b,\text{new}}\) and \(B = \bar b_\text{old} - A\,\bar b_\text{new}\). They are simple, but sensitive to a single unusual anchor. Characteristic curve methods. Stocking-Lord (Stocking and Lord 1983) chooses \(A\) and \(B\) to make the anchors’ test characteristic curve (the expected anchor score as a function of \(\theta\)) as similar as possible on the two scales. They use all the parameters at once and are more robust. An alternative to linking two separate calibrations is concurrent calibration: fit one multiple-group model to both forms, constraining the anchor items to be equal across groups and estimating the new group’s mean and standard deviation. Everything rests on the anchors behaving the same way in both administrations. An anchor whose parameters have changed, because it was exposed, taught to, or its position or wording changed, shows parameter drift, and it must be removed from the anchor set before linking. 10.2 Example 1: separate calibration and linking A language school has an old and a new 30-item placement test that share 10 anchor items. We simulate 1,000 students on each. The new cohort is stronger (mean 0.4, standard deviation 1.1), and anchor A06 was leaked and became easier on the new form. # Simulated NEAT design: old form (O01-O20 + anchors A01-A10) and new form # (N01-N20 + the same anchors); anchor A06 drifts on the new form. set.seed(1010) anchors <- sprintf("A%02d", 1:10) pars <- data.frame(item = c(sprintf("O%02d", 1:20), sprintf("N%02d", 1:20), anchors), a = rlnorm(50, 0.15, 0.25), b = rnorm(50, 0, 1)) gen <- function(items, n, mean, sd, shift = NULL) { p <- pars[match(items, pars$item), ] if (!is.null(shift)) p$b[p$item %in% names(shift)] <- p$b[p$item %in% names(shift)] + shift out <- simdata(matrix(p$a), matrix(-p$a * p$b), N = n, itemtype = "2PL", Theta = matrix(rnorm(n, mean, sd))) colnames(out) <- items as.data.frame(out) } old <- gen(c(sprintf("O%02d", 1:20), anchors), 1000, 0, 1) new <- gen(c(sprintf("N%02d", 1:20), anchors), 1000, 0.4, 1.1, shift = c(A06 = -1.2)) Calibrate each form on its own: fit_old <- mirt(old, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) fit_new <- mirt(new, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) p_old <- coef(fit_old, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[anchors, c("a", "b")] p_new <- coef(fit_new, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[anchors, c("a", "b")] round(cbind(b_old = p_old[, "b"], b_new = p_new[, "b"]), 2) #> b_old b_new #> A01 -0.49 -0.90 #> A02 0.69 0.18 #> A03 -1.44 -1.74 #> A04 -0.13 -0.38 #> A05 -1.05 -1.53 #> A06 -0.43 -2.10 #> A07 -1.10 -1.51 #> A08 -0.62 -1.02 #> A09 1.14 0.65 #> A10 -1.82 -2.15 The anchors look easier on the new calibration, because the new students are stronger and their calibration puts them at mean 0. Before linking, check for drift. On a common scale the anchor difficulties should lie on a straight line: library(ggplot2) ggplot(data.frame(old = p_old[, "b"], new = p_new[, "b"], item = anchors), aes(new, old)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey70", formula = y ~ x) + geom_point() + geom_text(aes(label = item), nudge_y = 0.15, size = 3) + labs(x = "Difficulty, new calibration", y = "Difficulty, old calibration") + theme_mirtverse() Figure 10.1: Anchor difficulties in the old and new calibrations; items off the line may have drifted. A06 sits well off the line formed by the others. A simple rule is to flag anchors whose difference in difficulty is far from the typical difference: diff_b <- p_old[, "b"] - p_new[, "b"] round(sort((diff_b - median(diff_b)) / mad(diff_b)), 1) #> A04 A03 A10 A08 A01 A07 A09 A05 A02 A06 #> -1.3 -0.9 -0.7 -0.1 0.0 0.0 0.7 0.7 0.9 10.8 We drop A06 from the anchor set and compute the mean-sigma constants from the remaining nine: keep <- setdiff(anchors, "A06") A <- sd(p_old[keep, "b"]) / sd(p_new[keep, "b"]) B <- mean(p_old[keep, "b"]) - A * mean(p_new[keep, "b"]) c(A = A, B = B) #> A B #> 1.04 0.44 \(B\) estimates how much stronger the new cohort is on the old scale (we simulated 0.4), and \(A\) how much more spread out (1.1). Stocking-Lord finds the constants that make the two anchor characteristic curves agree: tcc <- function(a, b, theta) sapply(theta, function(t) sum(plogis(a * (t - b)))) grid <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 41) sl_loss <- function(k) { A <- k[1]; B <- k[2] sum((tcc(p_old[keep, "a"], p_old[keep, "b"], grid) - tcc(p_new[keep, "a"] / A, A * p_new[keep, "b"] + B, grid))^2 * dnorm(grid)) } sl <- optim(c(1, 0), sl_loss)$par c(A = sl[1], B = sl[2]) #> A B #> 1.05 0.41 Both methods recover the cohort difference well. What would have happened if we had kept the drifted anchor? A_all <- sd(p_old[, "b"]) / sd(p_new[, "b"]) c(A = A_all, B = mean(p_old[, "b"]) - A_all * mean(p_new[, "b"])) #> A B #> 0.963 0.487 One leaked item is enough to distort the link, and with it every score on the new form. 10.3 Example 2: concurrent calibration and equating a pass mark Concurrent calibration fits both forms at once. We stack the two datasets; each student has NA for the items they did not take. # The same NEAT data stacked: NA for items not on a student's form. # A06 is renamed on the new form, so it is not treated as an anchor. new_a <- new; names(new_a)[names(new_a) == "A06"] <- "A06_new" resp <- merge(transform(old, form = "old", id = seq_len(nrow(old))), transform(new_a, form = "new", id = nrow(old) + seq_len(nrow(new_a))), all = TRUE) form <- factor(resp$form, levels = c("old", "new")) resp <- resp[, setdiff(names(resp), c("form", "id"))] Renaming A06 on the new form turns it into two separate items, one per form, which is the usual way to drop a drifted anchor from the link without discarding its responses. multipleGroup() constrains every item to have the same parameters in both groups (each unique item is only seen by one group anyway) and frees the new group’s mean and variance: mg <- suppressWarnings( multipleGroup(resp, 1, group = form, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE, invariance = c(colnames(resp), "free_means", "free_var"))) coef(mg, simplify = TRUE)$new[c("means", "cov")] #> $means #> F1 #> 0.411 #> #> $cov #> F1 #> F1 1.12 The new group’s mean and variance are estimated on the old group’s scale, and are close to the values we simulated (0.4 and \(1.1^2 = 1.21\)). Now the pass mark. The old form’s pass mark was 18 correct out of 30. What score on the new form corresponds to the same ability? IRT true-score equating finds the \(\theta\) at which the old form’s expected score (its test characteristic curve) equals 18, then reads off the new form’s expected score at that \(\theta\). items <- coef(mg, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$old$items old_items <- c(sprintf("O%02d", 1:20), anchors) new_items <- c(sprintf("N%02d", 1:20), setdiff(anchors, "A06"), "A06_new") tcc_form <- function(ids, theta) tcc(items[ids, "a"], items[ids, "b"], theta) theta_cut <- uniroot(function(t) tcc_form(old_items, t) - 18, c(-4, 4))$root c(theta_cut = theta_cut, new_form_cut = tcc_form(new_items, theta_cut)) #> theta_cut new_form_cut #> 0.419 19.763 curves <- data.frame(theta = rep(grid, 2), score = c(tcc_form(old_items, grid), tcc_form(new_items, grid)), form = rep(c("Old form", "New form"), each = length(grid))) ggplot(curves, aes(theta, score, colour = form)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_vline(xintercept = theta_cut, linetype = 2) + geom_hline(yintercept = 18, linetype = 3) + labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Expected number correct", colour = NULL) + theme_mirtverse() Figure 10.2: Test characteristic curves of the old and new forms on the common scale, with the cut score. If the new form is easier, its curve lies above the old form’s and the pass mark on the new form is higher; if it is harder, the pass mark is lower. Here the new form is a little easier, so the old pass mark of 18 corresponds to about 19.8 on the new form. Rounding the equated score to a whole number is a policy decision: rounding down passes slightly more candidates than the old standard, rounding up slightly fewer. 10.4 Your turn Repeat the mean-sigma link in Example 1 with the mean-mean method: \(A = \bar a_\text{new} / \bar a_\text{old}\), \(B = \bar b_\text{old} - A\,\bar b_\text{new}\). How close are the constants to the Stocking-Lord ones? Rerun the concurrent calibration of Example 2 with A06 as an anchor. How much does the estimated mean of the new group change? Compute the pass mark on the new form if the old pass mark were 22. A board member asks why the pass mark changed from one year to the next “when the standard was supposed to stay the same”. Answer in two sentences. Solutions A_mm <- mean(p_new[keep, "a"]) / mean(p_old[keep, "a"]) c(A = A_mm, B = mean(p_old[keep, "b"]) - A_mm * mean(p_new[keep, "b"])) #> A B #> 1.025 0.422 resp_all <- merge(transform(old, form = "old", id = seq_len(nrow(old))), transform(new, form = "new", id = nrow(old) + seq_len(nrow(new))), all = TRUE) form_all <- factor(resp_all$form, levels = c("old", "new")) resp_all <- resp_all[, setdiff(names(resp_all), c("form", "id"))] mg_all <- suppressWarnings( multipleGroup(resp_all, 1, group = form_all, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE, invariance = c(colnames(resp_all), "free_means", "free_var"))) coef(mg_all, simplify = TRUE)$new$means #> F1 #> 0.54 theta22 <- uniroot(function(t) tcc_form(old_items, t) - 22, c(-4, 4))$root tcc_form(new_items, theta22) #> [1] 23.1 With A06 treated as an anchor, the new group’s mean rises well above the simulated 0.4. The model has to explain why the new students do so much better on A06; since A06 is constrained to be the same item, part of the leak is credited to the students’ ability. Every new-form score would be too high. For example: “The standard is the same level of ability, not the same number of questions. This year’s form was a little easier, so reaching that level of ability takes a slightly higher number of correct answers.” In the lab Lab 4, run_lab("linking"), asks why a licensure exam’s pass rate jumped on a new form. You calibrate both forms, link them, check the anchors, compare separate and concurrent calibration, and carry the pass mark over. Chapter 11 Item banks, test assembly and adaptive testing Learning goals. After this chapter you can describe what an item bank stores and what it is for; read a bank’s information curve and spot where the bank is thin; assemble a fixed form from a bank under content constraints; explain, step by step, how a computerized adaptive test (CAT) selects items, scores people and decides when to stop; judge a CAT design by its precision, test length and item exposure. Key terms: item bank, automated test assembly, parallel forms, computerized adaptive test, multistage test, exposure. 11.1 The ideas Once items have been calibrated on a common scale (Chapter 10), their parameters can be stored in an item bank together with their content codes, usage history and review status. Because the parameters are on one scale, any selection of items from the bank yields scores on that scale. That makes two things possible. Automated test assembly (ATA) picks items for a fixed form so that the form meets a blueprint (for example, ten items from each content area) and its information curve matches a target: high at a cut score for a licensing test, flat across the range for a progress test (Linden 2005). Exact solutions use mixed-integer programming; simple greedy rules, which add the best remaining item that still fits the blueprint, often get close. A computerized adaptive test (CAT) goes further and builds a different test for every person while they take it (Wainer et al. 2000). The loop is: Start with a provisional \(\theta\) (often 0). Choose the unused item with the most information at the current \(\theta\), subject to content and exposure rules. Score the response and update \(\theta\) (usually by EAP, which works even after one item). Stop when the standard error is small enough or a maximum length is reached; otherwise go back to step 2. A CAT typically reaches the precision of a fixed test with half as many items or fewer. The price is a bank large enough to cover the whole range, and exposure: without control, the most informative items are given to almost everybody and soon become known. A multistage test (MST) is a compromise: people take pre-assembled modules, and the next module depends on their performance on the last one. 11.2 Example 1: a vocabulary bank and a fixed form A language-assessment centre has a calibrated bank of 200 vocabulary items in four areas. # A calibrated 2PL item bank: 200 items, four content areas. set.seed(1111) bank <- data.frame(item = sprintf("V%03d", 1:200), area = factor(rep(c("Everyday", "Academic", "Workplace", "Idioms"), each = 50)), a = rlnorm(200, 0.2, 0.3), b = c(rnorm(50, -0.8, 0.9), rnorm(50, 0.4, 0.9), rnorm(50, 0, 0.9), rnorm(50, 0.9, 0.7))) The bank’s information curve, overall and by area, shows where it can measure well: item_info <- function(a, b, theta) { p <- plogis(a * (theta - b)); a^2 * p * (1 - p) } grid <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.1) bank_info <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(bank$area), function(ar) { s <- bank[bank$area == ar, ] data.frame(area = ar, theta = grid, info = sapply(grid, function(t) sum(item_info(s$a, s$b, t)))) })) library(ggplot2) ggplot(bank_info, aes(theta, info, fill = area)) + geom_area() + labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Bank information", fill = NULL) + theme_mirtverse() Figure 11.1: Information of the 200-item vocabulary bank, stacked by content area. The bank is rich in the middle and thin at the extremes, especially below \(\theta = -2\) and above \(\theta = 2\). Everyday vocabulary covers the low end, idioms the high end. Item writers should be asked for very easy and very hard items. Now a 24-item fixed form with six items from each area, to measure well between \(\theta = -1\) and \(\theta = 1\). A greedy assembly adds, one at a time, the item that adds the most information at the target points, as long as its area is not yet full: assemble_greedy <- function(bank, length, per_area, targets) { chosen <- integer(0) while (length(chosen) < length) { full <- names(which(table(bank$area[chosen]) >= per_area)) cand <- setdiff(which(!bank$area %in% full), chosen) gain <- sapply(cand, function(i) sum(item_info(bank$a[i], bank$b[i], targets))) chosen <- c(chosen, cand[which.max(gain)]) } bank[chosen, ] } form <- assemble_greedy(bank, length = 24, per_area = 6, targets = c(-1, 0, 1)) table(form$area) #> #> Academic Everyday Idioms Workplace #> 6 6 6 6 Compared with a random 24-item form that meets the same blueprint: random_form <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(bank, bank$area), function(s) s[sample(50, 6), ])) se_at <- function(f, theta) 1 / sqrt(sapply(theta, function(t) sum(item_info(f$a, f$b, t)))) round(rbind(assembled = se_at(form, c(-1, 0, 1)), random = se_at(random_form, c(-1, 0, 1))), 3) #> [,1] [,2] [,3] #> assembled 0.265 0.236 0.276 #> random 0.318 0.304 0.332 The assembled form measures more precisely at all three target points with the same length and blueprint. For real programmes, assemble_forms() in the mirtverse assessment pipeline solves the same problem exactly, builds several parallel forms at once and handles enemy items (items that must not appear together). 11.3 Example 2: a CAT from scratch We now write a complete CAT in about 30 lines, using the same bank. The scoring step computes the EAP estimate on a grid of quadrature points, with a standard normal prior. quad <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 81) prior <- dnorm(quad) eap <- function(a, b, x) { like <- sapply(quad, function(t) prod(ifelse(x == 1, plogis(a * (t - b)), 1 - plogis(a * (t - b))))) post <- like * prior / sum(like * prior) est <- sum(quad * post) c(theta = est, se = sqrt(sum((quad - est)^2 * post))) } cat_one <- function(true_theta, bank, se_stop = 0.3, max_items = 30, top = 1) { used <- integer(0); x <- integer(0); est <- c(theta = 0, se = 1) while (length(used) < max_items && est["se"] > se_stop) { info <- item_info(bank$a, bank$b, est["theta"]); info[used] <- -Inf best <- order(info, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(top)] item <- if (top == 1) best else sample(best, 1) # randomesque exposure control used <- c(used, item) x <- c(x, rbinom(1, 1, plogis(bank$a[item] * (true_theta - bank$b[item])))) est <- eap(bank$a[used], bank$b[used], x) } list(theta = est[["theta"]], se = est[["se"]], n = length(used), items = used) } Simulate 300 test takers across the ability range. (To run the CAT on your own bank, replace bank in the data chunk of Example 1; it needs columns item, area, a and b.) # Simulated test takers for the CAT: one true theta per person. set.seed(1112) true_theta <- rnorm(300) runs <- lapply(true_theta, cat_one, bank = bank) res <- data.frame(true = true_theta, est = sapply(runs, `[[`, "theta"), se = sapply(runs, `[[`, "se"), n = sapply(runs, `[[`, "n")) c(mean_length = mean(res$n), rmse = sqrt(mean((res$est - res$true)^2)), cor = cor(res$est, res$true)) #> mean_length rmse cor #> 12.337 0.292 0.959 On average the CAT reaches a standard error of 0.3 with far fewer than 30 items. Test length depends on where a person is: in the middle, where the bank is rich, the CAT stops quickly; at the extremes it runs out of informative items and goes to the maximum. ggplot(res, aes(true, n)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + labs(x = "True theta", y = "Items administered") + theme_mirtverse() Figure 11.2: Number of items administered by the CAT against true ability. Exposure is the other side of the coin. With pure maximum-information selection, a few items are given to a large share of test takers: exposure <- function(runs) { table(factor(unlist(lapply(runs, `[[`, "items")), levels = 1:200)) / length(runs) } exp_max <- exposure(runs) sort(round(exp_max, 2), decreasing = TRUE)[1:6] #> #> 31 100 97 67 135 140 #> 1.00 0.68 0.64 0.60 0.48 0.48 The first item is the same for everybody (the most informative item at \(\theta = 0\)), so its exposure is 100%. The randomesque method picks at random among the five most informative items, which spreads exposure at a small cost in test length: set.seed(1113) runs_r <- lapply(true_theta, cat_one, bank = bank, top = 5) exp_r <- exposure(runs_r) rbind(max_info = c(max_exposure = max(exp_max), mean_length = mean(sapply(runs, `[[`, "n"))), randomesque = c(max_exposure = max(exp_r), mean_length = mean(sapply(runs_r, `[[`, "n")))) #> max_exposure mean_length #> max_info 1.000 12.3 #> randomesque 0.677 12.9 Content balancing (for example, cycling through the four areas) works the same way: restrict the candidate items before choosing the most informative one. simulate_cat() in the assessment pipeline runs this kind of simulation on a real bank, and the mirtCAT package can deliver an operational CAT. 11.4 Your turn Add 20 hard items (\(b \sim N(2.2, 0.4)\)) to the bank in Example 1 and redraw the information curve. What happens to CAT length for the most able test takers? Change the stopping rule to \(SE < 0.25\). How do mean length and RMSE change? Add content balancing to cat_one() so that each test has at least four items from every area. (Hint: while an area has fewer than four items, restrict the candidates to that area.) An admissions officer asks why two applicants got different questions and different numbers of questions. Write a short explanation. Solutions set.seed(1114) hard <- data.frame(item = sprintf("H%02d", 1:20), area = factor("Idioms", levels(bank$area)), a = rlnorm(20, 0.2, 0.3), b = rnorm(20, 2.2, 0.4)) bank2 <- rbind(bank, hard) top <- true_theta > 1.5 mean(sapply(lapply(true_theta[top], cat_one, bank = bank2), `[[`, "n")) #> [1] 14.8 mean(res$n[top]) #> [1] 17.8 runs25 <- lapply(true_theta, cat_one, bank = bank, se_stop = 0.25) c(mean_length = mean(sapply(runs25, `[[`, "n")), rmse = sqrt(mean((sapply(runs25, `[[`, "theta") - true_theta)^2))) #> mean_length rmse #> 18.963 0.246 The CAT reaches the target precision sooner for the most able test takers, because it now has informative items for them. Tests get longer and estimates more precise: precision costs items. For example: “The test adapts to each applicant: after every answer it picks the next question that tells us most about that applicant. Everyone is measured on the same scale, and the test stops when it has measured each person precisely enough, which takes fewer questions for some people than for others.” In the lab Lab 5, run_lab("cat-design"), asks whether a college should replace its fixed math placement test with a CAT. You examine the bank, run a CAT by hand, simulate it, and set exposure, content and stopping rules. Further reading Wainer and colleagues (2000) give an accessible introduction to CAT; van der Linden (2005) covers optimal test assembly. References

Chapter 12 Cut scores, reporting and communicating results Learning goals. After this chapter you can describe the Bookmark standard-setting method and build an item map at a response probability of 0.67; turn a cut on the \(\theta\) scale into a raw-score cut; estimate classification accuracy and consistency at a cut score; report IRT results to people who do not use R, with a written summary, a report and a dashboard. Key terms: cut score, standard setting, response probability, classification accuracy, classification consistency, test characteristic curve. 12.1 The ideas A cut score divides a scale into categories such as pass and fail, or below basic, proficient and advanced. Where the cut goes is a judgement about what performance is good enough, made by people who know the content and the consequences. Standard setting is the family of structured procedures for making that judgement defensibly (Cizek and Bunch 2007). The Bookmark method is closely tied to IRT. Items are ordered from easiest to hardest in an ordered item booklet, where each item’s location is the \(\theta\) at which a test taker has a fixed probability (usually 0.67, the response probability RP67) of answering it correctly. Each panelist places a bookmark after the last item that a just-qualified candidate should master. The location of the bookmarked item is that panelist’s cut, and the panel’s cut is usually the median over panelists after several rounds of discussion. For a 2PL item, the RP67 location is \[\theta_{0.67} = b + \frac{\ln(0.67/0.33)}{a}.\] Once a cut is fixed on the \(\theta\) scale, two numbers describe how well the test sorts people. Classification accuracy is the proportion of people whose estimated category matches their true category. Classification consistency is the proportion who would be placed in the same category on two independent administrations of the test. Both can be estimated from a single administration using the scores and their standard errors (Rudner 2001). Finally, results have to be communicated. People who make decisions with test scores rarely read item parameters. They need a short, honest summary of what the test measures, how precisely, for whom it works, and what the scores mean. 12.2 Example 1: setting a proficiency standard A provincial Grade 6 science test has 36 items. We simulate a calibration on 2,500 students. # Simulated 36-item science test, 2,500 students. set.seed(1212) a <- matrix(rlnorm(36, 0.15, 0.25)); b <- sort(rnorm(36, 0, 1)) resp <- simdata(a, matrix(-a * b), N = 2500, itemtype = "2PL") colnames(resp) <- sprintf("S%02d", 1:36) mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) pars <- coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items booklet <- data.frame(item = rownames(pars), a = pars[, "a"], b = pars[, "b"]) booklet$rp67 <- booklet$b + log(0.67 / 0.33) / booklet$a booklet <- booklet[order(booklet$rp67), ] booklet$page <- seq_len(nrow(booklet)) head(booklet, 8) #> item a b rp67 page #> S02 S02 1.924 -1.473 -1.105 1 #> S01 S01 0.928 -1.827 -1.064 2 #> S03 S03 1.243 -1.387 -0.818 3 #> S05 S05 1.335 -0.955 -0.425 4 #> S06 S06 1.118 -1.011 -0.377 5 #> S04 S04 0.833 -1.090 -0.239 6 #> S08 S08 1.245 -0.741 -0.173 7 #> S10 S10 1.931 -0.488 -0.121 8 The ordered item booklet is booklet, one page per item. Suppose eight panelists, after two rounds of discussion, place their bookmarks for proficient on these pages: bookmarks <- c(20, 22, 21, 23, 22, 24, 21, 22) panel_cuts <- booklet$rp67[bookmarks] theta_cut <- median(panel_cuts) c(theta_cut = theta_cut, spread = sd(panel_cuts)) #> theta_cut spread #> 0.7943 0.0586 The standard deviation of the panelists’ cuts, divided by the square root of the number of panelists, is a rough standard error of the panel’s cut. It should be reported alongside the cut. Teachers and parents see raw scores, so we convert the cut with the test characteristic curve: the expected number correct at \(\theta\). raw_cut <- expected.test(mod, matrix(theta_cut)) c(theta_cut = theta_cut, expected_raw = raw_cut, raw_cut = ceiling(raw_cut)) #> theta_cut expected_raw raw_cut #> 0.794 24.583 25.000 How many students are classified as proficient, and how accurately? sc <- fscores(mod, full.scores.SE = TRUE) above <- sc[, 1] >= theta_cut p_above <- pnorm((sc[, 1] - theta_cut) / sc[, 2]) c(percent_proficient = mean(above), accuracy = mean(ifelse(above, p_above, 1 - p_above)), consistency = mean(p_above^2 + (1 - p_above)^2)) #> percent_proficient accuracy consistency #> 0.204 0.925 0.893 Accuracy compares each student’s category with where their true score probably lies; consistency asks how often two independent testings would agree (here approximated from each student’s posterior probability of being above the cut). Consistency is always the lower of the two, because both testings carry error. An item map makes the cut concrete for teachers: it shows which items a just-proficient student is likely to answer correctly (the items below the line). Printing the text of a few items on each side of the line is a good way to describe what proficient means. library(ggplot2) ggplot(booklet, aes(page, rp67, colour = rp67 <= theta_cut)) + geom_hline(yintercept = theta_cut, colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2) + annotate("text", x = 1, y = theta_cut + 0.15, label = "Proficient cut", colour = "#C0392B", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#2C5F8A", `FALSE` = "grey60"), labels = c(`TRUE` = "mastered at the cut", `FALSE` = "not yet")) + labs(x = "Page in the ordered item booklet", y = "RP67 location (theta)", colour = NULL) + theme_mirtverse() Figure 12.1: Item map of the ordered item booklet with the proficient cut score. In a real programme, item_map() and set_cuts() in the assessment pipeline produce the booklet, record the panel’s judgements, and report impact and classification statistics for several cuts at once. 12.3 Example 2: telling the story We return to the attitude scale from Chapter 8 to show the reporting tools on a different kind of instrument. # Four 4-category attitude items (scored 1-4), 392 respondents. resp <- Science select_model() and interpret() give a plain-language summary that is a good first draft for the methods and results sections of a report: sel <- select_model(resp, verbose = FALSE) interpret(sel$best) #> Overview #> -------- #> * A graded model with 1 dimension was fitted to 392 respondents and 4 items #> (EM estimation). #> * The estimation converged normally. #> #> Model fit #> --------- #> * Overall model fit is poor: C2 = 19.18, df = 2, RMSEA = 0.148, CFI = 0.910, #> SRMSR = 0.073. #> #> Reliability #> ----------- #> * Marginal reliability is 0.67 (low). #> * Scores are too imprecise for decisions about individuals; consider adding #> items or using the scores only for group-level summaries. #> #> Targeting #> --------- #> * The average item location is -0.99 and the average person score is 0.00, so #> the test is relatively easy for this group. #> * Measurement is most precise around theta = -2.20 (information = 2.42, SE = #> 0.64). #> #> Items #> ----- #> * No items were flagged for low discrimination, extreme location, or misfit. #> #> Local dependence #> ---------------- #> * 1 item pair shows possible local dependence (Q3 exceeds the average of #> -0.19 by more than 0.2). #> * Strongest: Comfort & Benefit (Q3 = 0.08). #> * Check whether these items share a stimulus, wording, or content; consider a #> testlet or bifactor model. #> #> Person fit #> ---------- #> * 4.8% of respondents have unusual response patterns (Zh < -1.96), which is #> within what chance alone would produce. Read it critically before you use it: it flags the poor absolute fit and the low precision, and a careful report says what that means for the intended use of the scores. interpret_prompt() packages the same results into a prompt you can paste into an AI assistant to draft a longer narrative. Nothing is sent anywhere. For people who want to see everything, mirtverse writes a complete HTML report in one call, with the model comparison, the interpretation, tables, figures, a sum-score conversion table, item health cards and the code to reproduce it: mv_report(sel, file = "science-attitudes-report.html") For people who want to explore, a dashboard lets them move an ability slider, click through items and download tables, without R: mv_dashboard(sel$best, title = "Attitudes to science") export_dashboard(sel$best, "science-dashboard.html", format = "html") See Sharing results with a dashboard for the options. 12.3.1 A one-page memo Decision makers usually want one page. A structure that works: The question. What decision will the scores support? The answer. One or two sentences: can the test support it? The evidence. Three to five bullets: precision where the decision is made, classification accuracy, fairness checks, any items removed. What it means. The consequences of the cut for the people tested, for example the percentage classified in each category and how many are close to the cut. Recommendations and limits. 12.4 Your turn In Example 1, how many raw-score points does the cut move if every panelist moves their bookmark one page later? Repeat the item map with RP50 instead of RP67. Does the cut move up or down? Why does the choice of response probability matter to panelists? Add a second cut for advanced at page 30. Estimate the accuracy of the three-category classification. Write the “answer” and “evidence” parts of a memo about the proficiency cut in Example 1. Solutions cut_later <- median(booklet$rp67[bookmarks + 1]) c(expected.test(mod, matrix(theta_cut)), expected.test(mod, matrix(cut_later))) #> [1] 24.6 24.7 rp50 <- sort(booklet$b) c(rp67_cut = theta_cut, rp50_cut = median(rp50[bookmarks])) #> rp67_cut rp50_cut #> 0.794 0.100 adv <- median(booklet$rp67[rep(30, 8)]) cats <- cut(sc[, 1], c(-Inf, theta_cut, adv, Inf), labels = c("below", "proficient", "advanced")) p_cat <- cbind(pnorm((theta_cut - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2]), pnorm((adv - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2]) - pnorm((theta_cut - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2]), 1 - pnorm((adv - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2])) mean(p_cat[cbind(seq_len(nrow(p_cat)), as.integer(cats))]) #> [1] 0.88 Hardly at all here, because the items in that part of the booklet have very similar RP67 locations. Where the booklet has gaps between items, a single page can move the cut a lot, which is worth showing panelists. With RP50 every item’s location is lower, so the same bookmark gives a lower cut. Panelists must understand what “mastered” means (a 50% or a 67% chance), or their bookmarks will not mean what they intend. For example: “The test can support a proficient/not proficient decision. About 93% of students are expected to be classified correctly, and 89% would be classified the same way if tested again. The panel’s eight judgements were close together, and about one student in five is classified as proficient.” Use the numbers from your own output, and add the standard error at the cut (1 / sqrt(testinfo(mod, matrix(theta_cut)))). In the lab The course map ends with a final project: a full analysis of a dataset of the student’s choice, handed in as an mv_report() or a dashboard plus a two-page memo. The assessment pipeline is a useful checklist for it. Further reading Cizek and Bunch (2007) describe the Bookmark method and other standard-setting procedures. Rudner (2001) shows how to estimate classification accuracy from IRT results. The Standards (American Educational Research Association et al. 2014) set out what to report about cut scores. References

B Adapting the book for your course The book is meant to be changed. Each chapter is a separate R Markdown file, each example starts from one data chunk, and the book builds with one command, so you can reorder chapters, replace examples with your own data, or add a chapter for a topic you teach. The files All sources are in the book/ folder of the mirtverse repository: Table B.1: Source files of the book. File Contents index.Rmd Title page and preface 00-author.Rmd About the author 01-measurement.Rmd to 12-reporting.Rmd The twelve chapters, one per course week 90-datasets.Rmd, 91-adapting.Rmd The appendices _bookdown.yml Chapter order (rmd_files) and output folder _output.yml Look of the HTML, PDF and EPUB editions latex/ Title page, preamble and box styles of the PDF edition cover/ Cover artwork and how to regenerate it _common.R Code run before every chapter: loads mirtverse and sets chunk options references.bib References cited in the book The chapter files and their ids ({#measurement}, {#irt-models} and so on) are kept stable, so links to a chapter keep working across versions. Every chapter has the same shape A Learning goals box. Key terms, linked to the glossary. The ideas. Example 1 and Example 2, each starting with a data chunk labelled data-<chapter id>-1 or -2. Your turn, with solutions in a folded <details> block. In the lab and Further reading. Keep this shape when you add a chapter, and students will always know where to look. Swapping in your own data To use your own data in an example, replace the body of its data chunk and keep the label and the object names listed in Appendix A. For example, to run Example 1 of Chapter 2 on your own dichotomous test: ```{r data-irt-models-1} # Our midterm: 40 multiple-choice items, scored 0/1. resp <- read.csv("midterm-scored.csv")[, -1] # drop the ID column ``` The rest of the example then runs on your data. Two caveats: Examples built on simulated data compare estimates with the true values used to simulate them (objects such as true, true_theta or the planted DIF items). With real data there is no truth, so delete those comparisons or turn them into questions for students. The prose describes the original results. Re-read the text around each output after you swap the data, and edit the interpretation to match. The mirtverse instructor toolkit automates these steps, for example copying a chapter into a course folder and replacing a data chunk; see the instructor toolkit guide. Building the book Install bookdown once, then build from the book/ folder: install.packages("bookdown") bookdown::render_book("index.Rmd") # the whole book, into _book/ bookdown::preview_chapter("05-fit.Rmd") # one chapter, faster Open _book/index.html in a browser to read the result. The whole book builds in a few minutes on a laptop. To publish your own version, put the _book/ folder on any web server, or use GitHub Pages as the mirtverse repository does (its book workflow builds the book and publishes it next to the package website). Suggesting changes Every page has a Suggest an edit link at the top, which opens the chapter’s source on GitHub. Corrections and new examples are welcome as issues or pull requests in the mirtverse repository.
